messages.body_plain:
Fixed the problem.  Once I exported the data, and ran stan from a shell, I got the following helpful message:

Exception: INDEX OPERATOR [] OUT OF BOUNDS; index=5; lower bound=1; upper bound=4; index position=1; xi

Diagnostic information:
Dynamic exception type: std::out_of_range
std::exception::what: INDEX OPERATOR [] OUT OF BOUNDS; index=5; lower bound=1; upper bound=4; index position=1; xi

This told me that I was interpreting the statement

 vector[N] xi[k]

incorrectly.  I thought it meant a vector of N k-dimensional arrays, when in fact it is a vector of k N-dimensional arrays. Once I fixed that, it all worked.

It might be useful for those messages to pass through the rstan package somehow.

messages.subject: Correct use of truncated distributions
messages.body_plain:
Hi, I have a parameter matrix, t[i,j], declared as unrestricted (in range) in the parameters block and I over-ride the uniform priors by specifying a set of truncated normal distributions for t[i,j] in the models block (with the lower and upper truncation points differing for each (i,j) combination).   Will the specification of a truncated distribution in the models block automatically perform a jacobian adjustment to lp_ for HMC sampling associated with transforming the parameters, t[i,j], from restricted to unrestricted - or do I need to manually include the jacobian to transform from restricted to unrestricted (as shown on page 164 of the users manual)??    This question has broad applicability as the above case is probably the most common for employing truncated distributions.

Thanks, Terrance.

--
Thank you, Terrance Savitsky
messages.body_snippet: Hi, I have a parameter matrix, t[i,j], declared as unrestricted (in range) in the parameters block and I over-ride the uniform priors by specifying a set of truncated normal distributions for t[i,j] i

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Correct use of truncated distributions
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

You need not add the jacobian to lp__ if you are putting distributions directly on your parameters.

However, the problem in your case is you have an unrestricted parameter, but later you specify a restricted support on it.  This is problematic in Stan.  It is like the following simple *problematic* example.

parameters {
  real y;
}

model {
  y ~ uniform(0, 1); // problem: y is declared with support of the whole real line.
}

--
Jiqiang

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Correct use of truncated distributions
messages.body_plain:
Currently Stan cannot declare arrays where the element bounds are
different for different elements.  This can be worked around though.
For instance

data {
  real y_lower[5];
  real y_upper[5];
}

parameters {
  real<lower=0,upper=1> base_y[5];
}

transformed parameters {
  real y[5];
  for i = 1:5
    y[i] <- y_lower[i] + (y_upper[i] - y_lower[i])*base_y[i]
}

The only thing to be careful about is that if the upper and lower
bounds are also parameters and you want a uniform prior over the
values of y then you will need to explicitly declare the uniform
prior, it will not be implicitly handled in the right way without the
explicit declaration.

Cheers,
Marcus

Hi Marcus, Ben and Jiqiang,   Thank you for your quick and helpful responses and for your work to deliver Stan.  The approach Marcus suggests may work as it is scalable in size of the parameter matrix.  For example, I have something like a 20,000 x 25 parameter matrix whose values are restricted according to a data matrix of the same size and another set of ordered parameters.  The problem for me is that I would also like more distribution control (for identifiability and other reasons) for the resulting distribution on y[i] in Marcus' example.  I could replace the uniform on base_y with a more general beta distribution (or mixture of beta distributions) and that might do it, but it is an unorthodox approach (from the standpoint of producing publishable work).

My application is to build a data augmentation generating model for observed ordinal outcomes where a latent continuous response is restricted according to the observed ordered outcomes and a set of cutpoints.  If I employ a mixture model for the latent latent continuous response, then I can fix the cutpoints.   The vanilla implementation treats the cutpoints as random.  Stan does offer a solution for such problems that makes all of this go away by using the ordered_logistic distribution.  The problem is that one is then locked into a logistic distribution for the inverse link function.   The computational generality and power of Stan (vs. BUGS implementations) seems best deployed on more general and challenging models, however.

Terrance.

messages.subject: nested indexing
messages.body_plain:
Does STAN support nested indexing as a way to deal with missing/unbalanced data? In case my question is not clear, here's an example from the open bugs guide http://www.openbugs.info/Manuals/Tricks.html :

"Suppose we observe the following data on three individuals:

      Person 1: 13.2
      Person 2: 12.3 , 14.1
      Person 3: 11.0, 9.7, 10.3, 9.6

2. Nested indexing: Here the data are stored in a single array and the associated person is recorded as a factor, i.e.

       y[]   person[]
       13.2   1
       12.3   2
       14.1   2
       11.0   3
       9.7   3
       10.3   3
       9.6   3
      END

or list(y = c(13.2, 12.3, 14.1, 11.0, 9.7, 10.3, 9.6), person = c(1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3)).

A model such as y[k] ~ dnorm(mu[person[k]], 1) can then be fitted."

I agree.  The Cholesky factor basic type is
just easier.

The issue with covariance matrices is caching,
so the following operation would be efficient:

    matrix cholesky_factor(cov_matrix x);

(Right now, though, Stan doesn't include what kind of
matrix something is directly in the type checking.  The
reason is that we don't guarantee that a cov_matrix
remains a cov_matrix.  To do that, as we discussed before,
would require limiting the operations on it.)

Eventually, that could even use the Cholesky factor
basic type:

   cov_matrix_cholesky_factor
   cholesky_factor(cov_matrix x);

Then, I think the issue is how we cache the Cholesky
factor and recompute it if necessary in a lazy fashion.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Correct use of truncated distributions
messages.body_plain:
No, you can put whatever prior you want on the ys in the model block
(truncated or otherwise).  Though they are declared as unrestricted,
they are restricted in effect (because of their definition) and so
placing a truncated prior on them will be fine.  Note there are three
distinct but related issues at play here.

1. Ensuring that parameters lie in a proper range.  This can be done
by declaring them to have a proper range or constructing them in that
way.
2. Placing the correct prior on the parameters.  You can put any prior
you want on any parameter you want in the model block, however if you
are construct the parameters yourself (as I did in the example I sent)
then you can't fully rely on the implicit prior behaviour and should
declare it explicitly.
3. With truncated distributions in Stan if the range of the parameters
are not constrained to lie in the truncated range then the sampler is
likely to be very inefficient.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.body_plain:
Good call.  Totally my bad.  And it affects all of
the truncated distributions, not just the upper-bound
only.  None of these will work properly until we release
a patched version of Stan (and RStan), which we will do ASAP.

I just pushed a patch to our code repository that
fixes the issue, which is in stan/gm/generator.hpp,
starting on line 1024 or so.

We should set up a model test as the generator isn't
tested otherwise.

I forgot the negation due to the CDF terms being in
the denominator under a log.

An upper-truncated sampling statement

    y ~ foo(...) T[,U];

should translate to the C++:

    lp__ += foo_log(y,...);
    lp__ -= log(foo_cdf(U,...));

Because I inadvertently made the second line here += instead
of -= in the generator, we'll need to test this
through a model.

The other two cases we have are with just a lower
bound, using log1m(x) == log(1 - x), to set

    "" T[L,]
    lp__ -= log1m(foo_cdf(L,...));

and with both an upper and lower bound,

    "" T[L,U]
    lp__ -= log(foo_cdf(U,...) - foo_cdf(L,...));

An earlier thread brings up the issue of whether we
should try to be more careful about underflow of the CDF
to 0 or overflow to 1.  We could definitely be much
more careful with the arithmetical precision here.

We could really use three compound log-difference CDF
functions for these three cases.

We could then test if the lower bound was less than
the upper bound, something we're currently not doing.
As is, if they're backwards, you'll try to take the log
of a negative number and get an error that way.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On 9/4/12 5:47 AM, Marek Smigielski wrote:

 > I've just checked source version and still something
 > is suspicious in my opinion. Except of strange estimated parameter
 > values I get some exceptions.

The strange parameter values, assuming these aren't
what you were expecting, may be due to the model.
Let us fix the underlying distributions first, then we
can circle back and help fix the model if there are
still issues.

We're about to run some tests and release
a revised version of Stan and RStan.

The kinds of errors you're reporting below are
not fatal.  They occur when values underflow or
overflow out of range.  The sampler treats these
as zero probabilty and goes on its merry way.

If you only see a few, as you did here, it's not
a problem.  We're also working on making that
clear by changing "Error" to "Warning" in the report.
(What would be really nice is to link them back to
a line of the Stan source, but that's MUCH trickier
and not on our short-term to-do list.)

In general if you rebuild from source, you need to also
rebuild RStan, because RStan has the Stan code
built into it.

Circling back to your model:

 >      >     data {
 >      >       int<lower=0> N;
 >      >       real U;
 >      >       real<upper=U> y[N];
 >      >     }
 >      >     parameters{
 >      >       real mu;
 >      >       real<lower=0> sigma;
 >      >     }
 >      >     model {
 >      >       for (n in 1:N)
 >      >         y[n] ~ normal(mu,sigma) T[,U];
 >      >     }

First, you probably want a proper prior on sigma and on mu.
While Stan doesn't require a proper prior, it does require
a proper posterior.

Because the truncation point is data, it's not
actually doing anything in this model!  The data
are all known and constrained to be < U, so
T[,U] terms just add some constants of proportionality.

In order to properly estimate a truncated distribution,
you need to know the number of censored or truncated points.
See Gelman et al.'s Bayesian Data Analysis or Gelman and Hill's
regression book for information on how to code this kind
of thing into a model.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On 9/6/12 1:24 PM, Sean J Taylor wrote:
> I've been benchmarking Stan against JAGS for a simple logistic regression.  I have 2 binary independent variables and
> one binary outcome with 100K observations and 1500 groups.  For each model I am running 1000 iterations and 4 chains on
> a Macbook Pro with 2.4 Ghz processor.
>
> For a logistic regression, it takes about 6 minutes in Stan, 7 minutes in JAGS.  Not a bad speedup.

JAGS has a GLM module that can speed up some regressions.
I'm not sure if your model falls in that category or not.

> When I add random effects with a hyper parameter on the variance (tau ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001), u ~ normal(0,
> sqrt(tau)), u is a 1500 element vector), things slow down considerably.  Stan takes almost an hour to fit this model,
> whereas JAGS takes about 10 minutes.

Some questions:

1.  Were the number of effective samples similar when
you were done?

2.  What optimization are you compiling under?

3.  If you're not running under R, do you know what the
tuning parameters look like after adaptation and what
the tree depth is for NUTS?

4.  Does it take Stan a long time to converge to the
area of the final answer with a random starting point or
does it take a long time to sampler when it gets there?

> Am I doing something horribly wrong here?  I've attached my stan and bugs model files.

Not that I can see.  You have the right constraints
on the variance parameter tau.

One simplification you can make is to use the logit-scaled
Bernoulli, replacing

    z ~ bernoulli(inv_logit(theta))

with

    z ~ bernoulli_logit(theta);

It should be both faster and more arithmetically stable.

You might also try a slightly more informative prior on
the regression coefficients than normal(0,100); or you
could just drop the prior altogether -- the normal(0,100)
prior won't have much effect anyway.  But it also won't
lead to a big speedup.

Why do you have an inverse gamma prior on the variance tau?
That could be part of the problem, as the u are not very
cnstrained here.

See:

http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/taumain.pdf

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi Sean,

Another tip that I've found useful: Instead of saying

model {
  ...
  tau ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001);
  u ~ normal(0, sqrt(tau));
  ...
}

I'm confident you'll get faster convergence if you use this equivalent model:

transformed parameters {
  real u[J];
  for (j in 1:J)
    u[j] <- u_z[j] * sqrt(tau);
}
model {
  ...
  tau ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001);
  u_z ~ normal(0, 1);
  ...
}

The reason being that this breaks the strong prior dependence between
u and tau and reduces the range of the distribution of posterior log
probabilities. Of course, this kind of reparameterization might make
JAGS faster too, for all I know!

Best,
Matt

n 9/6/12 1:05 PM, Ben Domingue wrote:
> As a brief follow-up, I am getting better results with 3000 iterations. This somewhat surprises me given that the
> variances are always within the range of the prior...

After it converges, do you get decent effective
sample sizes?  If so, I'm guessing the problem is
in initialization.

That's a very fat uniform prior on the
variances, which doesn't provide much guidance.

With a range of [0,1000], the initial values Stan
generates randomly will be centered around 500.  It
can take a while to settle from overly high variances,
especially with the dependence in hierarchical models.

One tack you can take if you must have such a wide
prior is to provide more reasonable initializations
by hand.

- Bob

You have more effective samples than you probably need

stability as it gets around potential overflow and underflow

messages.subject: Problems with IRT model
messages.body_plain:
I discovered Stan through Andrew Gelman's blog two days ago. The description was enticing, so I installed it and started to play around.

I tried the "blocker" example of the BUGS manual vol 1 with no problems, and got a somewhat disappointing performance, when I compared it to the performance of JAGS on thsi very simple model. See attached blocker.(R|stan) file, which is annotated (and contains data).

Most of the elapsed time was spent in compilation. This did not really surprise me : I did not expect the heavy compilation process of Stan to be as fast as the light compilation offered by JAGS. I was more surprised buy the fact that, even using only one processor, sampling from an already fit model was about 30% faster in JAGS. But again, the overhead entailed by a compilation to C++ might easily explain this in the case of such a tiny model.

So I tried my hand at a problem I *knew* to be hard or JAGS : an IRT model (part of a larger model which can take *hours* to converge correctly on JAGS). This model follows largely Gelman & Hill's 2007 textbook.

My first attempt on a dataset containing missing values failed for reasons I have not yet understood (but I understand that the released stan 1.0.0 is not yet complete...). So I wrote another model dealing only with full data. This time, I got a runtime error complaining about a negative infinite log-likelihood, which I have been unable to trace. As far as I can tell, all my initialisations are reasonable.

Could you let me know where I goofed ? See ViStan.R for data and annotated source of calls and ViStan.stan and ViStanFull for the models.

Sincerely yours,
                                                                             Emmanuel Charpentier

Thanks for taking the time to try it and give us
feedback.

Responding to the note in the file, you're right that
Stan hasn't implemented random sample generation in the
generated quantities block.  We're working on it!
For now, you can do what you did and define it in the
model, which is definitely slower.

We'll be speeding up the model considerably when we
vectorize all the distributions.  This speedup will
scale with N.

> Most of the elapsed time was spent in compilation. This did not really surprise me : I did not expect the heavy
> compilation process of Stan to be as fast as the light compilation offered by JAGS. I was more surprised buy the fact
> that, even using only one processor, sampling from an already fit model was about 30% faster in JAGS. But again, the
> overhead entailed by a compilation to C++ might easily explain this in the case of such a tiny model.

When you say 30% faster, what exactly are you measuring?
Does that include the compilation time?  Are both Stan
and JAGS giving roughly similar effective sample sizes?
Everyone uses their own ESS estimator.

There's a note in the Wiki on how to up the optimization
level of R's built-in compiler to -O3 (optimization level
3).  That makes a big difference to Stan.  It slows
down compilation considerably, while at the same time
substantially speeding up sampling.

You should only have to compile a model once.

> So I tried my hand at a problem I *knew* to be hard or JAGS : an IRT model (part of a larger model which can take
> *hours* to converge correctly on JAGS). This model follows largely Gelman & Hill's 2007 textbook.
>

> that the released stan 1.0.0 is not yet complete...). So I wrote another model dealing only with full data. This time, I
> got a runtime error complaining about a negative infinite log-likelihood, which I have been unable to trace. As far as I
> can tell, all my initialisations are reasonable.

We're also planning to implement the models from
Gelman and Hill's book.  The one you did is
a pretty straightforward model with a discrimination
term.

> Could you let me know where I goofed ?

I don't see anything obviously wrong in terms of
what Stan expects.

Did you try letting Stan do the initialization?
Stan initializes randomly uniformly on [-2,2]
on the unconstrained scale.

Positive-constrained parameters like your gamma
get a log transform to unconstrain them, and exp
transform to come back; so initializing around 0 on
the unconstrained scale initializes around 1.

You can set init=0 to get all-zero inits on the
unconstrained scale.

The binomial(1,inv_logit(phi)) could be replaced with
bernoulli_logit(phi); I saw you did that in some other
models.  But Stan's pretty efficient at figuring out
which parts of the binomial calculation to do to get
the log probability up to a proportion.

 > ##   Error in function stan::prob::binomial_log<N4stan5agrad3varE>(N4stan5agrad3varE): Probability, theta, is nan:0,
 > but must be finite!

The error you report is likely to arise if theta is
never initialized.

## SAMPLING FOR MODEL 'IRT1' NOW (CHAIN 1).
## Erreur dans sampler$call_sampler(args_list[[i]]) : variable ImpCp missing

I hope this is self explanatory.  It's expecting to find
a variable and not finding it.  If you want to do missing
data models in Stan, they have to be coded differently than
in BUGS/JAGS.  There's a section in the programming part of
the manual with some examples.

I'll code up a version of the model you were trying
to debug and post it back to the list.

- Bob

Absolutely.  It won't be trivial given the read

Programmers often use "fu" (as in Kung Fu)

"i'm going to need crazy template juju for this".

compare ViStan.stan and ViStanFull.stan... I got inspiration from the manual for the handling of missing variables in ViStan.stan (the one which aimed to fit a model to data with incomplete observations).

messages.body_plain:
Le dimanche 9 septembre 2012 10:57:48 UTC+2, Shravan Vasishth a écrit :
> Hi,
>
> The manual says that the way to install Stan is:
>
>
> > To build Stan, first open a
> >
> > command-line terminal application. Then change directories to the directory in which
> >
> > Stan is installed (i.e., the directory containing the file named makefile).
> >
> > % cd <stan-home>
> >
> > Then make the library with the folloiwng make command.
> >
> > % make bin/libstan.a
>
> Here's the directory structure under stan-src-1.0.0 (below). There is no bin directory. In fact, there is no libstan.a anywhere under this directory.
>
> ls
> README.txt      lib             make            src
> TO-DO.txt       licenses        makefile        web
> doc             logos           rstan
>
> What am I doing wrong here?

Nothing.

Many programs use their arguments to specify their main input. E. g. "gcc foo.c" means "compile the C program foo.c" implicitly storing the relevant object file as foo.o).

"make" is different. Its main input is, by default,"makefile" in the current directory. If you open this file, you will see that this file defines targets and steps to obtain them. For example, one could have  makefile containing :

foo.o     foo.c
           gcc foo.c

makefile rules are intricate (see the man page for "make" to get a taste of it). In your case, "make bin/libstan.a" means "do whatever is necessary to build the target libstan.a in the bin directory, the steps being defined in the makefile". So type this exactly as written, and make will do its magic.

I'd recommend to take time to familiarize yourself with the Unix development environment, from where most of these tools come. They are command-line oriented, cryptic, as user-hostile as you can dream of, rather old by computer-science standards ... and frightfully powerful ! They became a de facto standard for development for good reasons...

HTH,

                                              Emmanuel Charpentier

> Shravan

just a warning) gets reported, we've lost the link to the
underlying variable in the Stan model.  It would be possible

>     and
>      > it's ok to initialize all the variables (then Stan will just use those inits), but it's not ok to initialize only
>     _some_
>      > of the variables?  If so, perhaps we should set Stan so that, if the user initializes some variables but not all,
>     Stan
>      > will automatically initialize the variables that the user did not initialize.
>      > Does this make sense?
>
>     Absolutely.  It won't be trivial given the read
>     routines, which are shared between data (which must
>     be there) and inits (which I agree would be better
>     the way you describe).  But it should be doable because
>     we know all the types and sizes of all parameters, so
>     we can calculate the number of unconstrained params to
>     fill in.  I can just drop flags through the code indicating
>     whether to fill in randomly or not.
>
>
> I second this position : initializing just the parameters that *must* have a  well-defined value is quite handy when you
> have a ton of parameters and only a few need precise initialization. I'd like to add that JAGS default behaviour for
> initialization (to 0, rather thn sampling from the prior as in OpenBUGS) seems to me more reasonable in many cases. I
> love the stan() R function range of options : "0", "random" or user-specified values. The best of ll worlds would be a
> named list of parameters, and a default, which could be either "0" or "random". But that might be treated at the R level.

That's what we're aiming for.  It'll take a bit of
work and there are other fires to put out at the
moment on basic error checking that we're going to
address first.

The biggest hurdle for the implementation is that the
inits are on the unconstrained scale.

I don't think JAGS always initializes to 0.  It says
in the manual that it takes reasonable values.
People like to use very fat priors even when they
have a good sense of what inits should be.  Maybe
Andrew has something to say about that -- he likes
dispersed initializations.

RStan and Stan use the same basic C++ code, but
they have different command-line controls for marshaling
the arguments.  The C++ needs the data to be given
to the model's class constructor and the constructor
computes the transformed data, all of which then remains
fixed throughout sampling.

So far, we haven't had problems with Stan converging,
even from pretty far-out inits.  If they do get so
bad that they result in NaN or infinite values, we
resample.

messages.subject: IRT models PL1, PL2 + multilevel versions
messages.subject_clean: IRT models PL1, PL2 + multilevel versions
messages.body_plain:
Item-response theory (IRT) models are very much the kind
of thing we had in mind when designing Stan -- it's essentially
a logistic regression with high correlation among
the parameters in the posterior.

I just wrote four Stan models for the basic IRT
models PL1 (aka Rasch) with no question discrimination
parameter and PL2 with the discrimination parameter, along
with multilevel variants of the kind described in Gelman
and Hill's regression book starting on p. 314.

You can browse the models online in our source repository:

https://code.google.com/p/stan/source/browse/#git%2Fsrc%2Fmodels%2Fmisc%2Firt

I tested them by generating data for 400 students
on 100 questions, with 25% of the data missing at
random.  This results in around 30,000 data points
and 500 (PL1) or 600 (PL2) parameters.

The models take about 5 seconds to compile in g++ at -O3
optimization.

Here's how long Stan took to warmup for 500 iterations
then sample for 500 iterations.  All models converged
to appropriate answers across multiple chains.

   PL1:  80 seconds (1m 20s)

   PL2: 180 seconds (3m 00s)

The hierarchical models took the same amount of time
as their non-hierarchical counterparts.

The PL2 models adapt to a smaller step size and more
steps, which is why they take longer (that and having
20% more parameters and their attendant differentiation
and updating).

It only consumes 14MB of memory peak, so there's no
problem running multiple processes concurrently.

I also ran on much more data.  Basic IRT for 1000 students
with 200 questions each (150K data points) ran
1000 warmup and 1000 sampling iterations (twice as many
as reported above) in 4 minutes in 70MB and converged to
the right answer.  I even ran basic IRT for 10,000 students with 200
questions each (1.5M data points), and though I lost
patience testing, I extrapolated about 2 hours for
1000 warmup and 1000 sampling iterations.  (I cut down
the later tests when I realized it was converging very
quickly from random inits.)

There's a bit of variation in the runs mainly due to
waiting for the step sizes to converge during warmup;
if the random initialization is far from a mode, especially
for the hierarchical parameters or intercept terms, then
it can take a bit longer to move to the mode because of
the need for reduced step sizes to keep the simulation
accurate (I never saw more than about 50% more time needed
than reported above).  With good inits it can run a bit faster than
reported above.

The notebook I tested this on is reasonably beefy:

   Mac OS X, Mountain Lion,
   2.3 GHz i7 CPU
   1600MHz DDR3 memory

Although I'm using the latest g++ from Xcode, version 4.21,
the latest from Macports is faster (as much as 20% in
some of our earlier tests of a version of 4.6 and they
continue to get faster).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Dear Bob,

Thank you for this effort. I have skimmed the stan files, and notice a couple of things :

1) You use one more parameter, the mean ability, whih, from a "sampling efficiency" point of view, should play the same role that the mean of the alpha distribution in Gelman & Hill's textbook.

2) You give to this mean an informative prior. This would be hard to defend against a reviewer.

3) Similarly, you give abilities, discriminations and difficulties somewhat informative priors. The same remark applies  : whereas imposing a standard deviation on abilities is just a choice of scale; imposing a small standard deviation to discriminations and difficulties *is* informative. Hard to do when you are exploring a situation where no prior knowledge has been formalized.

4) However, in the IRT2 hierrchical model, you do not state a prior for the abilities and difficulties. This, as far as I know, is equivalent to giving them the (improper) prior on (0, \infty), ths making the posterior improper, AFAIK. So much for model comparison...

In short, where Gelman & Hill's solution introduced both an additive and a multiplicative redundancy (by means of centering and scaling "raw" parameters), you keep the additive redundancy and replace the multiplicative redundancy by imposing more informative distributions.

I'll try to assess the impact of these choices by trying various values of the prior parameters.

Again, thank you !

                                                         Emmanuel Charpentier

You can put whatever priors you want on the
variables.  It doesn't affect the computation much.
It does affect the concentration of the posterior,
which is very sensitive to the choice of prior in
these models.

I also didn't provide a prior on the deviation
parameters, which I should probably do.

On 9/10/12 4:12 AM, Emmanuel Charpentier wrote:
> Dear Bob,
>
> Thank you for this effort. I have skimmed the stan files, and notice a couple of things :
>
> 1) You use one more parameter, the mean ability, whih, from a "sampling efficiency" point of view, should play the same
> role that the mean of the alpha distribution in Gelman & Hill's textbook.

Exactly.  You can parameterize it the other
way, but it's then adding a dependency to all the
parameters on the mean, which is less flexible than
just having the mean float.

> 2) You give to this mean an informative prior. This would be hard to defend against a reviewer.

Presumably in the same sense that any informative prior might
be hard to defend against a reviewer!

I could've added the priors as data as in the S. McKay Curtis
JSS paper on BUGS item-response models, so that they'd be
easier for users to play with.

I found when the priors were fatter than the values used
to simulate the data, the mean posterior estimates drifted
from their simulated values (in predictable, repeatable ways).

I'd recommend the hierarchical models, which don't have this
problem, but can also be difficult to defend against reviewers
in my experience.

> 3) Similarly, you give abilities, discriminations and difficulties somewhat informative priors. The same remark applies
> : whereas imposing a standard deviation on abilities is just a choice of scale; imposing a small standard deviation to
> discriminations and difficulties *is* informative. Hard to do when you are exploring a situation where no prior
> knowledge has been formalized.

Indeed.  As I said above, feel free to change the priors!

> 4) However, in the IRT2 hierrchical model, you do not state a prior for the abilities and difficulties. This, as far as
> I know, is equivalent to giving them the (improper) prior on (0, \infty), ths making the posterior improper, AFAIK. So
> much for model comparison...

Exactly -- the scale parameters have improper priors.
The posterior doesn't behave improperly, but I haven't done
a formal derivation.

Given how the model behaves without a prior (recovering
the true simulated values), and given the quantity of
data for the priors (# of questions, # of students), a
very weak prior shouldn't have much effect.

It's easy enough to add a prior.  Andrew likes using
weakly informative priors in these situations, but
I realize other researchers have different approaches.

> In short, where Gelman & Hill's solution introduced both an additive and a multiplicative redundancy (by means of
> centering and scaling "raw" parameters), you keep the additive redundancy and replace the multiplicative redundancy by
> imposing more informative distributions.

Gelman and Hill didn't propose a single solution.  They discuss
several methods (setting one value based on prior knowledge,
setting the mean to 0, then their actual model also sets the
scale to 1 by using a z-score type normalization).

I was just trying to use the simplest thing possible.

> I'll try to assess the impact of these choices by trying various values of the prior parameters.

Let us know what happens.  I don't have that much time to play
around with IRT parameterizations.

- Bob

One thing you can try is to use multi_normal_cholesky

I.E., add

transformed data {
matrix[N,N] A_chol;
A_chol <- cholesky_decompose(A);
}

then in the model

u ~ multi_normal_cholesky(0,sqrt(sigmasq_u)*A_chol);

Also, you should be able to use the vectorized version of the normal distribution. I.E., instead of the for loop over ys write

y ~ normal(beta0 + u, sqrt(sig2_e));

Cheers,
Marcus

> and 500 (PL1) or 600 (PL2) parameters.
>

> optimization.
>
> Here's how long Stan took to warmup for 500 iterations
> then sample for 500 iterations.  All models converged
> to appropriate answers across multiple chains.
>

>
>    PL2: 180 seconds (3m 00s)
>

> as their non-hierarchical counterparts.
>
> The PL2 models adapt to a smaller step size and more
> steps, which is why they take longer (that and having
> 20% more parameters and their attendant differentiation
> and updating).
>
> It only consumes 14MB of memory peak, so there's no
> problem running multiple processes concurrently.
>

> with 200 questions each (150K data points) ran
> 1000 warmup and 1000 sampling iterations (twice as many

> 1000 warmup and 1000 sampling iterations.  (I cut down

> quickly from random inits.)

> waiting for the step sizes to converge during warmup;
> if the random initialization is far from a mode, especially
> for the hierarchical parameters or intercept terms, then
> it can take a bit longer to move to the mode because of
> the need for reduced step sizes to keep the simulation
> accurate (I never saw more than about 50% more time needed
> than reported above).  With good inits it can run a bit faster than

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] random effects models with known covariance matrix
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] random effects models with known covariance matrix
messages.body_plain:
On 9/10/12 12:22 PM, f....@gmx.net wrote:
>...

> data {
>    matrix[N,N] A ;
>           ...
> }
>
> parameters {
>    vector[N] u;
>    real <lower=0> sigmasq_u;
>   ...
> }
>
> ...
> model{
> u ~ multi_norm(0 , A * sigmasq_u)
> }
>
> where A is the "numerator relationship matrix" and is known from pedigree, theory or from genomic marker data.
>
> Even for a relatively moderate size of N = 500 individuals, does STAN take extremely long to get in just 500 iterations,
> and for N = 1000, STAN will use up all of my 16 GB memory.
> This can't be, even if STAN is inverting A over and over again.

Unfortunately, it can be.  Because sigmasq_u is a parameter,
A * sigmasq_u is implicitly a transformed parameter.  That means
when the solver's run on it in this basic parameterization, it needs
to run an O(N^3) algorithm on it.  That generates O(N^3) subexpressions,
each of which requires approximately 12 bytes of storage.
The whole expression graph gets stored in order to evaluate
gradients.

With N = 500, that's 500^3, and I'm surprised you could get
Stan off the ground at all.

As Marcus suggested, the Cholesky parameterization will be
MUCH more efficient.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: multinomial_log: Sample sizes, ns,[1] is 0, but must be > 0!
messages.body_plain:
Hi

I'm running into a problem fitting data to a multinomial distribution when any of the observations are 0, which doesn't seem right.

I've made my model and data as simple as possible while still reproducing the error. If the model and code are

> library(rstan)
>
> island_model <- '
> data {
>     int<lower=0> A; // number of alleles
>     int<lower=0> J; // number of samples
>     int alleles[J,A]; // allele counts
> }
> parameters {
>     simplex[A] theta; // population frequencies
> }
> model {
>         for(j in 1:J)
>                 alleles[j] ~ multinomial(theta);
> }
> '
>
> alleles <- matrix(c(10, 10, 1,
>                     10, 13, 4,
>                     21, 28, 1,
>                     40, 19, 0), nrow=4, byrow=TRUE)

Then if I just use the first 3 samples

> fit1 <- stan(model_code=island_model, data=list(J=3,A=3,alleles=alleles[1:3,]), iter=1000, n_chains=4)

it works fine. However, if the fourth sample (40, 19, 0) is included

> fit2 <- stan(model_code=island_model, data=list(J=4,A=3,alleles=alleles), iter=1000, n_chains=4)

I get the error

> TRANSLATING MODEL 'anon_model' FROM Stan CODE TO C++ CODE NOW.
> COMPILING THE C++ CODE FOR MODEL 'anon_model' NOW.
> SAMPLING FOR MODEL 'anon_model' NOW (CHAIN 1).
>

messages.body_plain:
Just to reply briefly to this discussion:

I recommend never using improper priors.  Yes, we have an improper prior for the 8 schools but that's a well studied problem where we know the answer.  In general, it should always be possible to put a proper, weakly informative prior that constrains the parameters in a reasonable way without overwhelming your inference with prior information.

Note that there are no plans to write an *efficient* Gibbs or slice

custom-built Gibbs sampler.

Another thing to try (especially if RAM is the binding constraint) is to do the multivariate normal part yourself in the .stan file with

lp__ <- lp__ + whatever;

statements. If A_chol is fixed but sigmasq_u is a parameter, then sqrt(sigmasq_u)*A_chol is a parameter and multi_normal_cholesky() is doing a giant triangular solve every time the function gets called which also spews out a lot of autodiff calculations. If you invert A once at the outset (to get A_inv) and be careful not to divide by sigmasq_u too soon, it will go faster. Something like

lp__ <- lp__ - 0.5 * N * log(sigmasq_u); // non-constant part of log(det(sigmasq_u * A)^-0.5)
lp__ <- lp__ - (u' * A_inv * u) / ( 2 * sigmasq_u); // log of kernel of multivariate normal

Ben

With this latest version you should be able to write:

v ~ normal(0,sqrt(sigmasq_u));

And get almost exactly the same performance without having to muck
about with the log probability directly.

Or, alternatively, if you really care about getting the most speed
possible leave the lp__ statements as they are and  replace the loop

>  sum_of_squares <- 0.0; // or sum(pow(v, 2)) may / should work
>  for(i in 1:N) {
>    sum_of_squares <- sum_of_squares + pow(v[i], 2);
>

with

sum_of_squares <- dot_product(v,v);

which will be a fair bit faster than the loop, particularly for large N.

Cheers,
Marcus

> for(i in 1:I) {
>      y[i] ~ multi_normal(b[i] * x[i],sigma_y);
>    }
>    ...
> }
> |
>
>
> In R, I would expect
> |
> b[i,] %*% x[i,,]
> |
>
> to give me the correct vector. In stan, if I understand correctly, this code won't work because x[i] is a
> two-dimensional array of reals, not a proper matrix. Can I coerce it to be a matrix? Alternately, could I make x a
> vector of matrixes?
>
> Or should I just always flatten everything to two dimensions as most?

The simplest relevant declarations would be:

    row_vector[J] b[I];  // b is an I-array of J-row-vectors

    matrix[J,K]   x[I];  // x is an I-array of (JxK)-matrices

though you could also define b with the same effect as:

    matrix[I,J] b;

We followed MATLAB, not R/BUGS in our matrix operators,
so you can just use:

    (b[i] * x[i])'

to produce a column vector (b[i] * x[i] is a row vector).

We are going to generalize multi_normal in an upcoming
release to allow row vectors (as well as 1D arrays)
of matching dimension as well as vectors as arguments.

You can also save a transpose by storing x in the opposite
order, with:

    matrix[K,J] xt[I];  // xt[i] = x[i]'

    vector[J] bt[I];     //

In this arrangement, (xt[i] * bt[i]) is a column vector
so you don't need the transpose.  (You could even define
xt as transformed data so you could use the original data
coding.)

- Bob

messages.subject: Stan and RStan 1.0.1
messages.body_plain:
We are happy to announce the release of
Stan/RStan 1.0.1.  See:

   http://mc-stan.org/

1.0.1 is a patch release that fixes some major issues
with assignments to parameters, truncated probability
functions, visibility of functions within the modeling
language, and several minor issues.

The manual has also been double-checked to make
sure all of the code compiles and to incorporate all the
typo fixes people have submitted (thanks again!).

On the horizon, in addition to bug fixes, we have prioritized
vectorizing the remaining probability functions, adding more
cumulative distribution functions, adding new data types
to support multivariate analysis including constraints on
vector and matrix types, adding basic discrete sampling,
and parallelizing calls to Stan.

Please don't hesitate to contact the user's group
mailing list with questions, comments, or suggestions.

- Stan Development Team

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: STAN question?
messages.body_plain:
The seg fault is probably coming from the generated
model.  But that's not the root cause of the model's
problem (see below for at least one problem in the model
specification).

We should have eliminated all the seg faults from
the models by the next release.  The two places they
can occur now (version 1.0.1) when there are indexes out of
bounds of the arrays/vectors/matrices on the left-hand side
of assignment statements (<-) or when matrix operations are
applied to the wrong size arguments (e.g., trying to multiply
a 3x2 matrix by a 5x7 matrix).

Gianluca -- the code in your transformed parameters
block is wrong.  You have:

 >>     transformed parameters {
 >>       vector[2] phi;
 >>       vector[3] beta2;
 >>       vector[3] beta3;
 >>       vector[R] prob;
 >>
 >>       phi[1] <- phi_fix;           // need this trick because phi[1]=0 (if no migration stock data present) and
 >>       phi[2]~Normal(0,100) (if data on migration stocks present)
 >>       phi[2] <- phi_var;

The problem is that Stan does not work like BUGS (see
the new appendix for an overview of some differences).
When Stan execute the second statement,

  phi[2]~Normal(0,100) (if data on migration stocks present)

phi[2] has not yet been defined (we initialize to NaN).
So the result is going to be

    lp__ <- lp__ + normal_log(NaN,0,100);

so that the log probability will become NaN and never recover.

That's not the cause of the seg fault, but it's definitely
a bug in the model specification.

We try to describe how the transformed parameters work and
the parameters work in the manual.

Several of these user examples have been very
complex.  I'm thinking we need some way of debugging
models step-wise.  It's a big project, but it might
pay off with tracking down this kind of bug, which should
be pretty obvious under stepwise evaluation.

Jiqiang -- I don't think we need to go to the trouble
of writing simulations for user models to help them
with debugging.  Great if you have the time, but we
also have other things to do!

- Bob

>
> We should have eliminated all the seg faults from
> the models by the next release.  The two places they
> can occur now (version 1.0.1) when there are indexes out of
> bounds of the arrays/vectors/matrices on the left-hand side
> of assignment statements (<-) or when matrix operations are
> applied to the wrong size arguments (e.g., trying to multiply
> a 3x2 matrix by a 5x7 matrix).
>
> Gianluca -- the code in your transformed parameters
> block is wrong.  You have:
>
>
> >>     transformed parameters {
> >>       vector[2] phi;
> >>       vector[3] beta2;
> >>       vector[3] beta3;
> >>       vector[R] prob;
> >>
> >>       phi[1] <- phi_fix;           // need this trick because phi[1]=0 (if no migration stock data present) and
> >>       phi[2]~Normal(0,100) (if data on migration stocks present)
> >>       phi[2] <- phi_var;
>
> The problem is that Stan does not work like BUGS (see
> the new appendix for an overview of some differences).
> When Stan execute the second statement,
>
>
>  phi[2]~Normal(0,100) (if data on migration stocks present)
>
> phi[2] has not yet been defined (we initialize to NaN).
> So the result is going to be
>
>    lp__ <- lp__ + normal_log(NaN,0,100);
>
> so that the log probability will become NaN and never recover.
>
> That's not the cause of the seg fault, but it's definitely
> a bug in the model specification.
>
> We try to describe how the transformed parameters work and
> the parameters work in the manual.
>
> Several of these user examples have been very
> complex.  I'm thinking we need some way of debugging
> models step-wise.  It's a big project, but it might
> pay off with tracking down this kind of bug, which should
> be pretty obvious under stepwise evaluation.
>
> Jiqiang -- I don't think we need to go to the trouble
> of writing simulations for user models to help them
> with debugging.  Great if you have the time, but we
> also have other things to do!

It wouldn't be difficult in the sense that it'd just
be a big block of prints within an if statement in the
command code.

The nice part of such a list is that it would be
guaranteed to match the list of functions for the release
the user was using.  The not so nice part of such a list
is that we'd have to keep it in synch.  So far we have:

1.  actual function definitions in C++
2.  function_signatures specification for Stan parser
3.  LaTeX manual documentation

and we want to add

4.  LaTeX manual cheat-sheet short lists

and perhaps

5.  a list spit out using --functions on stanc

The only difficulty is in maintenance -- making sure the
list printed by stanc using a --functions flag matches
what we really have.

I'm also not convinced that the ASCII output would
be that readable, but hey, neither is the output for
"man g++" or even "man tar".

Andrew's already requested a few such tables for the manual.
I'm going to look at auto-generating the table as
a kind of index structure in LaTeX once I figure out how to format
the argument and result types.  If at the same time I can
generate a matching ASCII file of functions, then adding
a flag to stanc to spit out the functions would make sense.

One issue in such a list is how to list vectorized function
signatures.  I'm just using the pseudo-type "reals" in the manual,
which can match simple scalars, scalar arrays, and Eigen
vectors or row vectors.

On Friday, September 14, 2012 11:34:46 AM UTC-4, Ben wrote:
> Howdy all,
> I've wrapped the few examples I've been working with into the attached
> monstrousity. To offer a little context, this paper is the jumping off
> point:
> http://www.gllamm.org/BIOMtwins_08.pdf

Thank you.

> PS-While I'm writing, I have two add'l questions:
> 1. I'm wondering if there are plans to add the skew-normal
> distribution to the distributions one can access.

To the extent there are "plans", they are usually referenced in TO-DO.txt in the top level of the Stan directory, which can also be read at

https://code.google.com/p/stan/source/browse/TO-DO.txt

In general, we plan to add more distributions, although I have not heard of any mention of the skew-normal. However, adding a distribution to Stan is probably one of the easiest ways to contribute, even if you know very little C++. Just copy

src/stan/prob/distributions/univariate/continuous/normal.hpp

to

src/stan/prob/distributions/univariate/continuous/skew_normal.hpp

Then, hack skew_normal.hpp to add the skewness parameter (say alpha). Finally, you need to expose the skew_normal distribution to the parser, which we can help you with when the time comes.

Alternatively, it is possible to use any (log) density that can be written in closed form inside the .stan file using the

lp__ <- lp__ + whatever;

syntax. In the case of the skew-normal,

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skew_normal_distribution#Definition

you can just utilize the (log) normal density and add this line to the model{} block

lp__ <- lp__ + log(normal_cdf(alpha * x));

provided that alpha is defined in the parameters{} block. But you presumably want an informative prior on alpha to prevent alpha * x from going into a region of the parameter space where log(normal_cdf(alpha * x)) cannot be evaluated accurately in floating point arithmetic.

> 2. This block of stan code:
>   vector[ni] vA;
>   real sum_of_squaresA;
>   vA <- t_LA_inv * uA;
>   #
>   sum_of_squaresA <- dot_product(vA,vA);
>   lp__ <- lp__ - 0.5 * ni * log(var_l2A); // non-constant part of log(det(var_l2A * A)^-0.5)
>
>   lp__ <- lp__ - sum_of_squaresA / (2 * var_l2A); // log of kernel of multivariate normal
>
> magically leads to sampling of the uA random effects. I'd be really
> interested in knowing more about how this happens.

This was primarily intended to ease the computational burden that Frank was up against when the A matrix was fixed but huge. In general, one could simply use the non-magic

u ~ multi_normal(mean_vector, var_l2A * A);

However, this was wasteful in Frank's case because var_l2A is an unknown parameter in which case var_l2A * A is an unknown parameter in which case Stan needs to invert var_l2A * A and carry thousands of auto-differentiation sub-expressions to calculate the partial derivative with respect to var_l2A. We can avoid this by noting that

(var_l2A * A)^-1 = (1/var_l2A) * A^-1

and further noting that A^-1 is a constant iff A is a constant. Unfortunately, at the moment Stan does not have a parameterization of the multivariate normal in terms of the precision matrix; it is only parameterized in terms of the covariance matrix. Thus, we have to implement the desired parameterization of the (log) multivariate normal density within the .stan file. See

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multivariate_normal#Non-degenerate_case

There are several mathematically equivalent ways of proceeding that differ in computation time. Note that Frank's prior mean vector is zero, so we can ignore that part. The simplest way is to write

sum_of_squares = u' * A_inv * u;

However, this calculation does not exploit the fact that A_inv is symmetric, nor does it exploit the fact that the gradient wrt u is known to be A_inv * u. So, Stan would have to eventually arrive at this fact via the chain rule.

It is better to exploit the fact that

A_inv = L * L'

where L is a Cholesky factor of A_inv, in which case

u' * A_inv * u = u' (L * L') * u = v' * v

where v = L' * u. This formulation is helpful to Stan in two ways. First, L' has all zeros in its upper triangle so when it is post-multiplied by u, Stan does not waste (much) time multiplying elements of u by zero and more importantly does not add constant branches to the expression tree that it uses to calculate the gradient wrt u. Second, Marcus implemented a special version of dot_product(v,v) that is faster and uses less memory. It would be even better if we exposed the dot_self(v) function to the parser, but at the moment we don't.

At this point, the elements of the transformed vector v (or vA as you call it) are each distributed univariate normal with variance var_l2A, so you could just write

vA ~ normal(0, sqrt(var_l2A));

but Marcus says it is slightly faster to not do that an instead add the lines

sum_of_squaresA = dot_product(vA,vA);

lp__ <- lp__ - 0.5 * ni * log(var_l2A); // non-constant part of log(det(var_l2A * A)^-0.5)
lp__ <- lp__ - sum_of_squaresA / (2 * var_l2A); // log of kernel of multivariate normal

Note that

- sum_of_squaresA / (2 * var_l2A) = - 0.5 * u' * (var_l2A * A)^-1 * u

which is the kernel of the (log) multivariate normal density. But we also have to remember that det(var_l2A * A) is a function of the unknown parameter var_l2A, which is reflected in the second line. But we do not want to literally calculate that determinant (or any determinant of a dense matrix if we can avoid it). Thus, we use the identity for the determinant of a scalar times a matrix given at

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Determinant#Properties_of_the_determinant

and take the log to get - 0.5 * ni * log(var_l2A).

Ben

I hope someone else who's better at multivariate modeling

> PS-While I'm writing, I have two add'l questions:

We're waiting for user feedback on what to add.  It's
pretty easy at this point for us to add vectorized log
probability functions -- around a person day or less with
testing.  Is there an R function somewhere you trust we
can use to generate unit tests?  (Once we get some basic
values we trust, then we can use the function itself to
test the gradients with finite differences.)

The CDFs for truncation can be much trickier, because
we want to be able to differentiate w.r.t. the parameters
as well as the outcome.

> 2. This block of stan code:

> multivariate normal
> magically leads to sampling of the uA random effects. I'd be really

I'm not sure what exactly you're asking.  There's
a description of how Stan works in the manual.

The basic idea is that lp__ is the log probability accumulator.
You can write an entire Stan model without ~ by incrementing
lp__ directly.  We then automatically differentiate the function
defined by the model and use it in NUTS.  There's a transform
step for constrained variables, too.  And like other Metropolis
algorithms we only need the log probability function up to a
proportion.

- Bob

see if the problem goes away?

the data you're running that's problematic (feel
free to use e-mail:  st...@mc-stan.org.

We've gotten around some of these in the logit case
by writing a logit-parameterized density function
directly (just for bernoulli, but we'll add binomial).

messages.subject: hierarchical mixture modelling
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

I'm trying to implement a hierarchical mixture model and I was hoping
to get some help with a few sticking points I've encountered thus far.
I've created a gist (https://gist.github.com/3734783) that has R code
for explaining/generating the data that I'm attempting to model. The
gist also has my attempt thus far at coding the stan model.

2 Technical questions:

1) How would I go about defining the VonMises distribution for use in
Stan? (In R, I just use the rvm() and dvm() functions from the
CircStats package.)

2) Does it look like I implemented the mixture appropriately? I tried
to understand and extend the mixture example from the docs, but I
might have missed something.

And a more theory-related question:

So far the data-generating R code and stan fitting code assumes zero
covariance amongst the three parameters that get sampled per "person"
("person_rho", "person_mu", "person_kappa"). Sampling of person_rho
and person_kappa are both from Gaussians, so I could use
multi_normal() as illustrated in the docs to estimate the covariance
between these parameters. However, where person_mu is sampled from a
VonMises, I'm guessing there's no way to simultaneously estimate all 3
covariances? In this case, I guess I could still use multi_normal() to
estimate the covariance between person_rho and person_kappa, then
simply assume that the other 2 covariances are zero (coincidentally,
I'm not *as* interested in those covariances anyway). However, I
wonder if I should be concerned about any influence on the accuracy of
inference this assumption might have if it is violated by the data.
Thoughts?

Another solution might be to give up use of the Von Mises for
representing the distribution of person_mu values; my data is unlikely
to have dramatic variability in person_mu values (they're likely all
pretty close to zero), so I suspect I could get away with using a
Gaussian. Though presumably in this case I'd still need to ensure that
the sampled person_mu values are constrained to the finite range (-pi
to pi) that mu can take, which I'm guessing might be achieved by
sampling the Gaussian on the real then transforming the result
(something like: inverse_logit(sample)*2*pi-pi ). In this case,
however, I'm not sure how to extend the docs example of using
multi_normal() in the 2-parameter case to the 3-parameter case;
specifically, do I need to do anything to ensure that sigma is
positive definite?

Thanks to anyone who suffered through this long post,

Mike

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology
Dalhousie University

Looking to arrange a meeting? Check my public calendar: http://goo.gl/BYH99

~ Certainty is folly... I think. ~

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] hierarchical mixture modelling
messages.body_plain:
The model looks pretty close to what you'd need.

Just a couple of sticking points in the loop:

   real ps[2];
   for (t in 1:T) {
       ps[1] <- log(person_rho) + log(vonMises(person_mu,person_kappa));
       ps[2] <- log(1-person_rho) + log(uniform(-pi(),pi()));
       lp__ <- lp__ + log_sum_exp(ps);

First, you want to replace the term

   log(uniform(-pi(),pi()))

with

   uniform_log(person_mu, -pi(), pi());

The notation uniform(L,H) is for when there is a sampling
statement, as in:

   person_mu ~ uniform(-pi(), pi());

This just translates into a form that calls the three-argument
uniform_log() function.

Next, you can eliminate the ps[2] local variable and just
use the binary log_sum_exp function and simplify the loop to:

   for (t in 1:T) {
       lp__ <- lp__ + log_sum_exp(log(person_rho) + log(vonMises(person_mu,person_kappa)),
                                  log(1-person_rho) + uniform_log(person_mu,-pi(),pi()));

But person_mu isn't constrained to lie in (-pi, pi) in the model,
and if it's a mixture of von Mises and uniform, the uniform needs
to have all of the person_mu in its support or you'll get an error
when evaluating the uniform_log.

Now as for how to do the von Mises, that looks a bit
sticky, because there's a (log) Bessel function of
order 0 that depends on the concentration parameter:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Von_Mises_distribution

Now if we had Bessel functions available in Stan, you could
code the distribution as with the mixture by incrementing
the log probability accumulator lp__ appropriately.  Or if
the concentration parameters were constant, you could do
the same but drop the Bessel term.

What we would need to do to support Bessel functions would
be to write a C++ implementation of the function and its
derivative.  I think we'd just need order 0 and order 1
functions.  Looks like Boost provides a generic implementation
for any order, so it shouldn't actually be too hard:

http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_51_0/libs/math/doc/sf_and_dist/html/math_toolkit/special/bessel/bessel.html

I'll add it to our function to-do list.  Maybe someone will
take it up sooner rather than later.

By the way, this is also what we'd need to add the
von Mises distribution to Stan, which would save you the
work of coding its density.

- Bob

messages.subject: rstan warmup samples
messages.body_plain: >From reading the docs/watching the sampling output, my understanding is that rstan obtains iter number of samples (all of which are saved), with warmup number of those used for adapting the sampler. If this assumption is correct, how do I ignore the warmup samples that are saved when making inference (say for something as basic as printing the summary of the fit)? And is it possible to have rstan simply not save these warmup iterations?
messages.body_snippet: >From reading the docs/watching the sampling output, my understanding is that rstan obtains iter number of samples (all of which are saved), with warmup number of those used for adapting the sampler.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] rstan warmup samples
messages.body_plain:
In RStan, all are saved.  But the warmup samples are not used for summary and print.

Now, there is no option not to save the warmup iterations.  However, the extract function can get draws without warmup by specifying inc_warmup = FALSE.

Jiqiang

messages.body_plain:
I patched the bug in type inference for constrained
vectors (simplex, ordered) and matrices (covariance
matrices, correlation matrices).  The fix was
pushed to Google code in commit:

   commit 5179786a67fd53a1f995bd2131eeb50e69b1fd9d
   Author: Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com>
   Date:   Tue Sep 18 15:24:03 2012 -0400

   fixed issue with hidden dims for corr_matrix, cov_matrix, simplex, and ordered

Until our next official release, putting any of these constrained
vector or matrix types in an array makes them invisible to the code.
There's not a good workaround because the constraints are necessary.

If you want to work with the above commit tag, it's good
to go from Git.

It was another "C++ isn't like Java" bug that bit me.
I redeclared member variables on the constrained subclasses
of matrix types, but called them through superclass refs,
so the correct ones were hidden.  I'm sort of surprised
lint didn't catch that -- the Java compiler issues a warning
if you hide variables like this.

Thanks again for the report and sorry again for the bug.

- Bob

> I think I am misunderstanding something. In the von Mises distribution,
>
> f(x | u,k) = e^( k * cos(x - u) ) / ( 2 * pi * I(k) )
>
> if we substitute the random variable y := cos(x - u), constrain y to be on
> [-1,1], unwind to get the transformed parameter x = acos(y) + u, and deal
> with the change of variables, then what is the problem besides implementing
> the log of the Bessel function(s)?

Note that acos : [-1,1] -> [0,pi] not -> [-pi,pi] so the range of x is
limited.  It also doesn't allow users to write x~vonMises(u,k) where x
is an angle because the transform is not generic on x, but is
dependent on the distribution parameter u.

To be clear the issue with the other obvious solution of constraining
x to be in [-pi,pi] is that it breaks the space such that transitions
from +pi to -pi are practically impossible with a general purpose
sampler like HMC/NUTS.

Cheers,
Marcus

On Wednesday, September 19, 2012 11:06:57 AM UTC-4, Daniel Mitchell wrote:
> Hi everyone, I've implemented (in C++) some circular probability distributions for my team and I would like to submit them for inclusion in stan/rstan. Can someone walk me through the process?

We should have a document outlining the process for contributions, but at the moment we don't. In general, if you are familiar with git, then the best thing is to point us to a branch or send a patchset to the list. But in cases like this where the contribution is an entirely new C++ file, like my_distribution.hpp, then it is fine to just attach the file to an email to this list.

Rough guidelines for adding a new distribution:

-- Look at a .hpp file for a similar distribution that is already in stan (somewhere under src/stan/prob/distributions ) and try to follow the same conventions. Some distributions accept vector inputs and for some distributions we supplement the auto-diff process with analytic derivatives, but this is not absolutely essential at the outset. In other words, a slow but correct log density is better than nothing.

-- In general, it is important that the density work both for fixed inputs (data) and parameter inputs. We use templates in C++ to handle these different cases, but sometimes there is a lot of somewhat obscure code going on to implement all this.

-- Try to also add some tests (look under test/prob/distributions and test/agrad/distributions for examples) that verify that the log density evaluates to something that matches an external algorithm (such as that in an R package)

-- Document the new density in the .tex files under src/docs/stan-reference/ .

-- The last step is to expose the new distribution to the parser so that it can be used in .stan files. This involves editing  src/stan/gm/function_signatures.hpp and maybe some other stuff. We can help you with this when you get to this step.

But, overall. anything you can do to get the process started is a step in the right direction and if the new density is in demand, someone will work with you to get it across the finish line.

Thanks,
Ben

Two more issues.

One, you want to run to convergence, say all R-hat values
under 1.1 or so.

Second, you need to constrain parameters to match their
support in the model:

>> parameters {
...

>> real<lower=0> sigma_beta1; // variances des coefficients
>> real<lower=0> sigma_beta2;

...
>> model {
...

>> sigma_beta1 ~ uniform(0, 1000) T[0,];
>> sigma_beta2 ~ uniform(0, 1000) T[0,];

sigma_beta1 and sigma_beta2 should be declared
as real<lower=0,upper=1000>.  At this point, the
uniform distribution is implicit, but adding
it to the model won't hurt (Stan's smart enough
not to do the redundant calculations).

You  should eliminate these truncation statements,
though, as they're redundant.  Restriction of
variables to a range happens in their declarations
in the parameters block.  Truncation just changes
the distribution.

- Bob

I just sketched out a way for users to add
their own distribution code without having them
built into Stan.  But it'll be a few revisions
before this is in the code base.  Even after it
is, we're still happy to take donated code and
integrate it.

On 9/19/12 11:06 AM, Daniel Mitchell wrote:
> Hi everyone, I've implemented (in C++) some circular probability distributions

As we've discussed recently (I can't recall if
it was on stan-dev or stan-users), sampling
circular distributions are problematic for Hamiltonian
Monte Carlo (of which NUTS is an instance).  The
issue is that the manifold of values (here the
circle) can't be projected continuously into R^N.

If you only need a data distribution

   y ~ circular(theta)

where y is known, there's no problem.  But if y
can be variable, there's an issue with projecting
the circle to R^N.

 > for my team and I would like to submit
> them for inclusion in stan/rstan. Can someone walk me through the process?

We're rather light on process per se and I'm
not sure what you mean by "in C++".  Are they
integrated into Stan already or is it just
an implementation of a density for double/int
args?

As to submission, you just need to go along with
the BSD license.  We're going to have to figure out
whether we keep adding copyright holders.  The
Eigen

If you want to see how our distributions are
written, look at the code.  They're in:

    src/stan/prob/distributions/...

The biggest issues are:

   - no external dependencies other than Boost and
     Eigen

   - independent template parameters for each
     scalar/vector/matrix argument (not int) in
     order to support auto-dif

   - error checking policies implemented a la Boost

   - propto calculations via type traits

   - google test unit tests of all of the above,
     including auto-dif tests and value tests

   - vectorization via expression templates, which you
     can see in normal.hpp;  this isn't mandatory, but
     it makes models way faster

   - cumulative distribution functions, which we'll need
     for truncated models;  also optional

If you're still interested after looking at the above,
drop us the code via e-mail:  st...@mc-stan.org
Or we can add you to the stan-dev list where we
discuss this kind of thing.

I'm happy to look at unintegrated code or git
diffs and provide feedback.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: Spatial distributions?
messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, September 19, 2012 6:21:32 PM UTC-4, John wrote:
> Has anyone tried to implement in Stan the kind of spatial distributions found in Geobugs, such as proper CAR?  Would Stan likely be much faster for these models?

A coauthor and I have been using one such model. The important thing to keep in mind is that Stan doesn't do conditional distributions, inclusive of the conditional autoregressive (CAR) distribution. Stan does joint distributions. Some flavors of BUGS implement CAR because it admits Gibbs sampling. Stan does variants of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. The implications of this difference are that 1) you can use whatever priors and distributional assumptions reflect your beliefs rather than the priors and distributional assumptions that lead to known full-conditional distributions and 2) you need to express your priors in terms of the joint distribution rather than the conditional distributions. In our case, it turned out that the normal CAR thing that we would have used if we were using BUGS corresponded to an improper multivariate normal joint distribution (improper because the covariance matrix was singular). And that eventually ran reasonably fast. Your case might well imply some other multivariate normal (or maybe t) with a nonsingular but structured covariance matrix. At the moment, the C++ code in Stan is a bit thin in this area. The multivariate normal and t distributions exist, but are not optimized for structured covariance (or precision) matrix. So, in order to get optimal speed, you might have to do some parts within the .stan file with

lp__ <- lp__ + whatever;

syntax. See the chapter called "Assignments" in the reference manual or this thread

https://groups.google.com/d/topic/stan-users/HcvYaDu71_Y/discussion

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Hi Marcus, You provided a trick (below) to allow separate restricted intervals for the elements of a vector or matrix, "y",  which will then have imposed a truncated (or restricted range) prior.   You point out that it may be wise to state an explicit prior on "y" in order to have a known distributional behavior, given that the trick is based on employing multiple parameter sets.  You also note that the truncation ranges on the prior should match the restricted values for "y" set via your trick for sampler efficiency.   I'm confused by why this set-up works to produce a correct model.  While the range for each element of "y" is restricted to the correct range by using your algorithm, "y" is still declared as unrestricted.   So how does Stan know to perform the transformation to unrestricted - with the accompanying Jacobian adjustment - for HMC sampling?  Is it the truncated prior that communicates the need to transform?  If so, then it seems like it would be correct to simply declare "y" as unrestricted (but initialize with values in the correct truncated range) and just employ a restricted distribution.   The issue would then be one of sampling efficiency, though the result would still be correct, right?

messages.body_plain:
> On Sep 19, 2012, at 6:26 PM, Richard McElreath wrote:
>
>> I've been translating a few ongoing data analysis projects into Stan code, mostly with success.

Let us know if you run into specific problems we
can help with.

>> Originally, I had written the sampler myself in raw R code. It was very slow, but I knew what it was doing at least.
>> Just before Stan version 1.0 was released, I had managed to get JAGS to do it all quite reliably. But JAGS was taking
>> a long time to converge and then producing highly autocorrelated output. Stan has been amazing, in comparison. I could
>> hardly believe the traceplots. Stan produces the same inferences as my JAGS code does, but with 8 hour runs (no
>> thinning needed) instead of 30 hour runs (with massive thinning).

That still seems like a long time!

In running in R and comparing speeds, is
everyone making sure to reset R's compiler
to use optimization level -O3?
Stan is MUCH faster with -O3 than with R's
default -O2 level (as will be anything else compiled
from source through R, so it's a good idea
even if you don't use Stan).

See the R getting started guide for instructions
on how to do it.

It's also important to make sure you're using
a version of JAGS compiled with -O3, by the way.

>> I'm confident that there are places where the speed and precision in my model code could be improved

 >> Many thanks for the effort behind Stan.

You're welcome.  We're very happy to see people making
good use of it.

See below.

>> Below is the framework for the zero-inflated model, abstracted to a simulated data example. I've put the model code
>> inline for convenience of reading, and then attached the full R script. The only real trick needed here is to replace
>> observed zeros with some positive real, so vectorized calculations on gamma density don't throw errors ("No acceptably
>> small step size could be found. Perhaps the posterior is not continuous?").

Is the problem on the branch of the if-else you're using?
The problem with if-else is that unlike a proper ternary
operator (cond ? valT : valF) which only evaluates the
expression valT if the condition is true and valF if
the condition is false, the if-else always evaluates
both because it's compiled to a function.

I'm going to write proper conditionals into Stan soon.

The code looks great.  I'm so happy people are figuring out
how to code complex (in Stan coding terms) models like this.

>> |
>>     data {
>>         int<lower=0> N;                 // number of cases
>>         int<lower=1> J;                 // number of clusters
>>         real<lower=0> y[N];             // observed outcome
>>         int<lower=0,upper=1> iszero[N]; // indicates a zero outcome
>>         int<lower=1> id[N];             // cluster number for each case
>>         cov_matrix[2] Omega;            // diagonal prior
>>     }
>>     parameters {
>>         vector[2] mu;                   // means of varying effects
>>         cov_matrix[2] Sigma;            // var-cov matrix for varying effects
>>         vector[2] alpha[J];             // varying effects for each cluster
>>         real theta;                     // log scale
>>     }
>>     model {
>>         real pi;                        // probability of zero GLM
>>         real mugamma;                   // mean of gamma GLM
>>         Sigma ~ inv_wishart( 3 , Omega );
>>         mu[1] ~ normal( 0 , 100 );
>>         mu[2] ~ normal( 0 , 100 );
>>         theta ~ normal( 0 , 100 );
>>         for (j in 1:J) alpha[j] ~ multi_normal( mu , Sigma );
>>         for (n in 1:N) {
>>             pi <- inv_logit( alpha[ id[n] , 1 ] );
>>             mugamma <- exp( alpha[ id[n] , 2 ] );
>>             lp__ <- lp__ + if_else( iszero[n] , log(pi) , log1m(pi) + gamma_log( y[n] , mugamma*exp(theta) ,
>> exp(theta) ) );

Once we've vectorized all the distributions, it'll be
easy to speed this up another factor of 2 or 3.  It's
our top priority right now.

I would've written your model as follows:

   real exp_theta;

   real mugamma;                   // mean of gamma GLM
   Sigma ~ inv_wishart( 3 , Omega );

   mu ~ normal(0,100);  // vectorized

   theta ~ normal( 0 , 100 );
   for (j in 1:J) alpha[j] ~ multi_normal( mu , Sigma );

   exp_theta <- exp(theta);

   for (n in 1:N) {

     iszero[n] ~ bernoulli_logit(alpha[id[n],1]);

     mugamma <- exp( alpha[ id[n] , 2 ] );

     for (i in 1:(1 - iszero[n]))
       y[n] ~ gamma(mugamma * exp_theta, exp_theta) );
   }

I pulled exp(theta) out of the loop, which will save
both memory and time.

The replacement of your pi terms with bernoulli_logit is
based on the definition:

   bernoulli_logit_log(u) = log(bernoulli(inv_logit(u)))

This should be faster, use less memory, and be more
arithmetically stable.

I'm sorry to say we don't have a proper conditional yet,
but I'm going to add one pretty soon.  Until then,

messages.body_plain:
On 9/19/12 9:29 PM, terrance savitsky wrote:
> Hi Marcus, ...   You also note that the truncation ranges on the prior should match the restricted values for

> "y" set via your trick for sampler efficiency.   I'm confused by why this set-up works to produce a correct model.
>   While the range for each element of "y" is restricted to the correct range by using your algorithm, "y" is still
> declared as unrestricted.   So how does Stan know to perform the transformation to unrestricted - with the accompanying
> Jacobian adjustment - for HMC sampling?

The parameters that HMC/NUTS sees are the unconstrained
versions of variables declared in the parameters block.

So declaring a 5-array of [0,1]-bounded parameters,
as in your example

 >     parameters {
 >        real<lower=0,upper=1> base_y[5];
 >     }

uses logit() to unconstrain to (-infinity,infinity).
What happens in the code is that the parameters are always
kept in the unconstrained space by the sampler and then
inverse transformed to their constrained variants,
here with inv_logit().  This means the log absolute
Jacobian for the n-th parameter is log(inv_logit'(y[n])),
and that is what gets added to the log probability
accumulator lp__ implicitly before the user code
executes over the constrained parameter which it
sees as base_y[n].

After that, setting the base_y[n] from the array into
a vector doesn't require a transform.

All of this clunkiness is because I haven't yet
implemented lower- and upper-bound constraints for
vector parameters.  But they're on the to-do list,
as I can see they're going to be more important for
vectorized operations than I'd originally anticipated.

> Is it the truncated prior that communicates the need to transform?

No.  Although the probability functions do check their
domains and throw exceptions if inputs are out of support.
That's why declarations with constraints are important.

> If so, then
> it seems like it would be correct to simply declare "y" as unrestricted (but initialize with values in the correct
> truncated range) and just employ a restricted distribution.   The issue would then be one of sampling efficiency, though
> the result would still be correct, right?

No, see above.

- Bob
