On Thursday, September 20, 2012 8:52:50 PM UTC-4, tds151 wrote:
> Interesting.  So eventually we won't lose computational efficiency by directly employing a covariance matrix built from a structured configuration in a multivariate normal distribution once a covariance matrix class is defined in C++?  The woodbury matrix identity wouldn't be employed, tho??

#include<forward_looking_statements_disclaimer>

Eventually, there will be an abstract covariance matrix class and a bunch of subclasses with specialized methods for common operations. The public attributes of the abstract covariance matrix class would be things like the correlation matrix, the standard deviations, the Cholesky factor, the precision matrix, the Cholesky factor of the precision matrix, etc. plus a bunch of flags indicating whether each attribute has been allocated yet. Then when some function needs one of these attributes to do some calculation, it would first have to check whether it has been allocated and if not, do it in an efficient way and then cache the result so that subsequent functions do not need to recreate it.

So, in your case, we might have an EFA structure covariance matrix class that inherits from the abstract covariance matrix class and has additional attributes for the loadings and unique variances. In which case, we would specialize the inverse() function to do Woodbury-based calculations (as opposed to Cholesky-based calculations for a generic covariance matrix or LU-based calculations for a generic square matrix). Similarly, we would create a function called quadratic_form() that takes a vector (x), a covariance matrix (Sigma), and a bool indicating whether to calculate x' * Sigma * x or x' * Sigma^-1 * x and it would spit out that sum of squares in the best way we know how for that class of covariance matrix.

So, for an AR1 structured covariance matrix class, there would be additional attributes for phi and sigma_squared. The inverse() function would be implemented analytically to exploit the tridiagonality and ideally would produce a sparse matrix. And quadratic_form() would exploit the bidiagonality of the Cholesky factor of the precision matrix, and so on.

> In my case re: the kronecker product, I use your approach to jujitsu my way out of direct computation of the kronecker product.   in particular, I directly augment lp__ with the matrix variate distribution of Dawid, where for a D x M parameter matrix, Y,  the matrix variate normal is notated with:
> Y - C ~ N(P,Q) where P is a D x D covariance matrix and Q is an M x M covariance matrix.   C is a D x M mean.
>
> The density is proportional to:  det(P)^{-M/2} * det(Q)^{-D/2} * exp(-0.5*trace[P^{-1} * Y * Q^{-1} * Y^{'}]).
>
> In my case, P is specified under a sparse, factor analytic construction.

You might look into the "bag of trace tricks" also. Taken literally, Stan will construct the whole matrix, P^{-1} * Y * Q^{-1} * Y^{'} , even though it only needs the diagonal to calculate the trace. If you define A' = P^{-1} * Y and B = Q^{-1} * Y^{'}, then

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trace_%28linear_algebra%29#Trace_of_a_product

says that trace(A' * B) is equal to the sum of the Hadamaard product. So, in Stan syntax it would be

sum(A .* B)

We use that trick in src/stan/prob/distributions/multivariate/continuous/{inv_}wishart.hpp .

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Hi Josef,

There are a number of things you can do to speed things up with your model.  One big thing you can do is use the vectorized form of the normal distribution.

E.G.,  instead of

  for(i in 1:max_word){
     word_mu[i] ~ normal(0, words_sigma);  // word effect

   }

and

  // b_coefs

  for(i in 1:n_bspline){
    b_coefs[i] ~ normal(0, 100);
    male_b_coefs[i] ~ normal(0, 100);
    c2_b_coefs[i] ~ normal(0, 100);
    c2_male_b_coefs[i] ~ normal(0, 100);
  }

you can simply write

word_mu ~ normal(0,words_sigma);
b_coefs ~ normal(0,100);
male_b_coefs ~ normal(0,100);
c2_b_coefs ~ normal(0,100);
c2_male_b_coefs ~ normal(0,100);

which should be a fair bit faster.

Your cumsum would probably be faster done as follows:

Instead of

  // This whole block is basicaly cumsum(delta[1:i])
  Delta[1,1,1] <- delta[1];
  Delta[1,1,2] <- delta[1] + c2_delta[1];
  Delta[1,2,1] <- delta[1] + male_delta[1];
  Delta[1,2,2] <- delta[1] + c2_delta[1] + male_delta[1] + c2_male_delta[1];

  for(i in 2:max_dob){
    Delta[i,1,1] <- Delta[i-1,1,1] + delta[i];
    Delta[i,1,2] <- Delta[i-1,1,2] + delta[i] + c2_delta[i];
    Delta[i,2,1] <- Delta[i-1,2,1] + delta[i] + male_delta[i];
    Delta[i,2,2] <- Delta[i-1,2,2] + delta[i] + c2_delta[i] + male_delta[i] + c2_male_delta[i];
  }
  //end cumsum

Use

  for(i in 1:max_dob){
    t0 <- sum(delta[1:i]);
    t1 <- sum(c2_delta[1:i]);
    t2 <- sum(male_delta[1:i]);
    Delta[i,1,1] <- t0
    Delta[i,1,2] <- t0 + t1;
    Delta[i,2,1] <- t0 + t2;
    Delta[i,2,2] <- Delta[i,1,2] + t2 + sum(c2_male_delta[1:i]);
  }

There may be a few others that can be done now but that's a start.  Right now indexing limitations will prevent making other big gains (e.g., vectorizing y or speaker_mu) but become available in the future.

Hope this helps.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.body_plain:
Bob,  I'd appreciate your help to think through a problem.   what i want to do is set truncation limits for t[i,d] based on y[i,d].   if y[i] = 1, then t[i,d] < gamma[d,1]  (where gamma is an array of ordered vectors).   if y[i,d] = number_of_categories, then t[i,d] > gamma[d,number_of_categories - 1]; otherwise gamma[d,y[i,d] - 1] <  t[i,d] <= gamma[d,y[i,d]].   the easiest way to impose the truncation boundaries without employing conditional statements is to just place -infinity and +infinity on the left and right ends of the gamma[d].   Of course, since I set the scale of t[i,d] (to identify the model) I may readily choose a value for abs(infinity) that will work - such as 1e3, for example, and that should work fine.  I just wanted to so something less hack-ish.   I suspected negative_infinity() / positive_infinity() wouldn't work unless the truncation recognized and turned off the boundary.

If I don't want to use this hack approach, I could try directly augmenting lp__ using if_else(), but I don't think it's flexible enough - since there are 3 possible outcomes that determine the update, not 2, and if_else() doesn't look like it is designed to chain or nest multiple if_else() checks.

Thanks, Terrance.

messages.subject: reading RStan models from files vs. strings
messages.subject_clean: reading RStan models from files vs. strings
messages.body_plain:
I strongly recommend using the

    file=<filepath>

argument to stan() in RStan to specify a model
from a file rather than the

    model_code=<string>

argument to specify the model as a string.

Whatever you do, don't cut and paste from a file
into a string.  Not only is it tedious, it's
error prone (c.f., Fitts's law).

I think people may not realize the file option is
there because the first example in the RStan getting
started guide uses a string rather than a file, as does
the example in the draft appendix of the 3rd edition
of BDA.

- Bob

No.  It's exactly the same.

> I realized there was the file option, but opted for the string approach because I preferred to keep as much of
> my code for this analysis in one place as possible.

Ah.  My motivation was to cut down cut-and-paste errors.
If you have an entire R script in a file along with
the model, that arrangement makes sense, too.

I tend to run models with different data, though, and
like to keep the following concerns separated:

    -- model
    -- R code (or other code) to munge data
    -- R code to call fit code (including inits)
    -- R code to draw plots and analyze
    -- one script to run everything for an analysis

The main reason is that I often run the same model over
data from different sources with different shapes and then
run different output analyses over them.

The style in R is to have one big function do everything,
which gives you nice encapsulation but lower flexibility,
whereas my arrangement is more unix-like, which is more
modular, but less encapsulated.

- Bob

On 9/21/12 1:53 PM, terrance savitsky wrote:
> Bob,  I'd appreciate your help to think through a problem.   what i want to do is set truncation limits for t[i,d] based
> on y[i,d].   if y[i] = 1, then t[i,d] < gamma[d,1]  (where gamma is an array of ordered vectors).   if y[i,d] =
> number_of_categories, then t[i,d] > gamma[d,number_of_categories - 1]; otherwise gamma[d,y[i,d] - 1] <  t[i,d] <=
> gamma[d,y[i,d]].

My head hurts just thinking about this.

There's no way to conditionally declare a variable
as having a lower bound, upper bound, or both.

 > the easiest way to impose the truncation boundaries without employing conditional statements is to
> just place -infinity and +infinity on the left and right ends of the gamma[d].   Of course, since I set the scale of
> t[i,d] (to identify the model) I may readily choose a value for abs(infinity) that will work - such as 1e3, for example,
> and that should work fine.  I just wanted to so something less hack-ish.   I suspected negative_infinity() /
> positive_infinity() wouldn't work unless the truncation recognized and turned off the boundary.

Right -- it won't work yet.

And it's a bit of a pain to add because
of the way integer vs. floating-point arithmetic
works and the way auto-dif works (not too bad, but
hours we don't have).  We'll add it soon as it's
the right limit behavior.

> If I don't want to use this hack approach, I could try directly augmenting lp__ using if_else(), but I don't think it's
> flexible enough - since there are 3 possible outcomes that determine the update, not 2, and if_else() doesn't look like
> it is designed to chain or nest multiple if_else() checks.

if_else() will certainly chain, but it's inefficient
in that it always evaluates both branches (unlike
C++'s ternary operator or a true branch).  You can
also use Marcus's hack I mentioned a day or two ago and
use

   int<lower=0,upper=1> bool_value;

   bool_value <- ...
   for (dummy in 1:bool_value)
      body;

The body only gets evaluated if bool_value = 1.

We'll add conditionals as soon as we get the lower-level
bugs sorted out.

- Bob

Terrance,

One thing that could be done is to separate your y variable into a y
with a lower bound, a y with an upper bound, and a y that is bounded
both below and above. I'm thinking along the lines of how we suggest
splitting observed data and missing data (covered in the manual).

If the bounds are fixed for each of those subsets, I think it should
work. The preprocessing can be done in R or perhaps a transformed data
block, as long as the bounds are conditional on data.

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Just so I understand the basics, this is what I understand from your advice:

1) I won't be eliminating any loops, but will be changing what's done inside of a loop.
2) It's less expensive to create a vector and assign values into it through a loop and then do the vectorized sampling, than it is to do the sampling inside of the loop.

Is that right?

-Joe

On Friday, September 21, 2012 4:14:33 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I was only looking for where the error in parsing/compiling
> came from.
>
> You can get a whole lot more efficiency by vectorizing
> the call to
>
> speaker_mu[i,j] ~ normal(...);
>
> Allocate a vector for the means, fill it with the mean
> values in a loop, then call vectorized normal all at
> once.  That means replacing this:
>
>    for (i in 1:max_speaker) {
>      for (j in 1:max_context) {
>        speaker_mu[i,j] ~ normal(Delta[dob[i],sex[i],j]
>                                   + (male_effect * (sex[i]-1))
>                                   + (context_effect * (j-1))
>                                   + intercept,
>                                 sigma);
>      }
>      speaker_sigma[i] ~ cauchy(0, 2.5) T[0,];
> }
>
> with this:
>
>
>   for (i in 1:max_speaker) {
>     real predix[max_context];
>     for (j in 1:max_context)
>       predix[j] <- Delta[dob[i],sex[i],j]
>                      + (male_effect * (sex[i]-1))
>                      + (context_effect * (j-1))
>                      + intercept;
>     speaker_mu[i] ~ normal(predix,sigma);
>   }
>
>   for (i in 1:I)
>      speaker_sigma[i] ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
>
> Note you don't need truncation because sigma's constrained
> to (0,inf) and we only need computation to a proportion (and
> those cumulatives are expensive!).
>
> You could also put it all in one big array, which is even
> faster, but requires loop fiddling.  We'll eventually get around
> to vectorizing to matrices, but we're doing vectors for
> everything first.
>
> And then the same trick with N, which is even more important
> if N is large relative to everything else:
>
>      for(i in 1:N){
>          y[i] ~ normal(speaker_mu[speaker[i], context[i]] + word_mu[word[i]], speaker_sigma[speaker[i]]);
>      }
>
> becomes
>
>     real predix2[N];
>     real spkr_sigma_spkr[N];
>     for (i in 1:N){
>       predix2[i] <- speaker_mu[speaker[i], context[i]] + word_mu[word[i]];
>       spkr_sigma_spkr[i] <- speaker_sigma[speaker[i]]);
>     }
>     y ~ normal(predix2,spkr_sigma_spkr);
>
> This is MUCH faster.  Basically, you can think of loops and assignments
> as basically free in Stan (they're compiled to efficient C++, unlike
> R or BUGS loops).  What's expensive is each ~ used and each complicated
> function used in an assignment.
>
> - Bob

messages.body_plain:
On 9/21/12 4:44 PM, Josef Fruehwald wrote:
> Just so I understand the basics, this is what I understand from your advice:
>
> 1) I won't be eliminating any loops, but will be changing what's done inside of a loop.
> 2) It's less expensive to create a vector and assign values into it through a loop and then do the vectorized sampling,
> than it is to do the sampling inside of the loop.
>
> Is that right?

Right.

It's not the loops that are expensive, it's the sampling
statements executed inside them.  Assignments and vector
allocations (implied by local variable declarations) are
relatively inexpensive (probably not even measurable as
a fraction of total work in cases like yours).

For reasons having to do with how automatic differentation
of the log probability function is done, it's MUCH MUCH
more efficient to call one vectorized sampling statement than
to call the individual sampling statements in a loop.
It saves substantial work in allocation, reduces memory
usage, and greatly reduces the number of virtual function
calls (the big bottleneck for modern CPUs is figuring
out where a program will branch to and a bunch of
very unpredictable virtual function calls is about as bad
as it gets for that).

For what it's worth, you can open the hood on JAGS and
add vectorized distributions there.  This provides a pretty
big speedup for similar reasons (they interpret loops and
function calls -- we interpret expressions during auto-dif).

- Bob

Thanks Bob and Daniel for your help.   Your approaches would work fine.  I would input bool_1, bool_2, bool_3 as data and then use the loop constructions Bob lays to ensure only the correct statements are executed.  Marcus had earlier provided me a workaround for declaring different restriction limits on a vector (or matrix) of parameters.   His workaround involves generating a same-sized vector of real<lower=0,upper=1> parameters and using lower and upper bounds generated as a function of a vector of (parameter) cutpoints and the data (as you suggested Daniel) to generate a transformed parameter vector.   The workaround anyway will require that i use -infinity and infinity for some of the lower an upper bounds in the parameter vector.   So I'm going to anyway have to employ the hack of creating a transformed data constant set to a large value to simulate infinity.   If I have to anyway do this, then I already have a workaround setting truncation limits in the assignment of the distribution that just involve augmenting a vector of cutpoints that involve placing +/- infinity on each end, respectively.  Then no conditional statements are required.   I was trying to avoid the hack of having to fix a large value for infinity, but it is unavoidable.

> >> to do is set truncation limits for t[i,d] based
> >> on y[i,d].   if y[i] = 1, then t[i,d] < gamma[d,1]  (where gamma is an
> >> array of ordered vectors).   if y[i,d] =
> >> number_of_categories, then t[i,d] > gamma[d,number_of_categories - 1];
> >> otherwise gamma[d,y[i,d] - 1] <  t[i,d] <=
> >> gamma[d,y[i,d]].
> >
> >
> > My head hurts just thinking about this.
> >
> > There's no way to conditionally declare a variable
> > as having a lower bound, upper bound, or both.
> >
> >
> >> the easiest way to impose the truncation boundaries without employing
> >> conditional statements is to
> >>
> >> just place -infinity and +infinity on the left and right ends of the
> >> gamma[d].   Of course, since I set the scale of
> >> t[i,d] (to identify the model) I may readily choose a value for
> >> abs(infinity) that will work - such as 1e3, for example,

> > Right -- it won't work yet.

> > And it's a bit of a pain to add because
> > of the way integer vs. floating-point arithmetic
> > works and the way auto-dif works (not too bad, but
> > hours we don't have).  We'll add it soon as it's
> > the right limit behavior.
> >
> >
> >> If I don't want to use this hack approach, I could try directly augmenting

> >> flexible enough - since there are 3 possible outcomes that determine the
> >> update, not 2, and if_else() doesn't look like
> >> it is designed to chain or nest multiple if_else() checks.
> >
> >
> > if_else() will certainly chain, but it's inefficient
> > in that it always evaluates both branches (unlike
> > C++'s ternary operator or a true branch).  You can

> > use

> >
> >   bool_value <- ...

> >

> >
> > We'll add conditionals as soon as we get the lower-level

messages.subject: Hierarchical (Conditional) Multinomial Logit Example
messages.body_plain:
First, I would like to thank the Stan team for this most generous gift! I can only imagine the time and effort that has gone into this project. So thanks.

I have been playing around with Stan and the results are impressive. I started with a Hierarchical Linear Regression (as a response to Ian's earlier question on imbalanced panels) and the results were great.
(Blog pose here: www.sanjogmisra.com/blog/stan/ <http://www.sanjogmisra.com/blog/stan/>)

Since then I have been playing around with a "real" example of a Hierarchical Multinomial Logit (Mixed Logit) as applied to a brand choice context (I'm in a business school!)
I have attached files for those who are interested.  The code works and the chains generated converge very fast (realtive to BUGS/JAGS). Having said that, I have run into some issues that I was hoping others (the Stan team) could help with:

a) The compilation and sampling time is somewhat long (my comparison code in JAGS compiles and samples much faster but doesn't mix as well).
b) At some points i get a "Non-Fatal" warning that the inverse Wishart draw is bad.

Warning (non-fatal rejection): Error in function stan::prob::inv_wishart_log<i>(i): W is not positive definite (0)

c) While the chain converges fast in most cases, once in a while the sampling slows to a crawl and the resultant chain shows poor mixing (see attached pdf where chain #1 has poor mixing). Not sure why this happens. Sometimes the acceptance rates drop quite a bit even after the chain seems to have gotten to the "correct" parameter range.

Any and all other thoughts are welcome. I am in the process of benchmarking Stan with JAGS, BUGS and available code in R but wanted to make sure I get the most efficient version before I do so. My guess is that I could vectorize my code better but cant seem to figure out how.

Some Notes:
I am using the -O3 flag.
I have tried using the multinomial distribution (rather than lp__) that doesn't help speed things up.
I have tried the multi_normal_cholesky (doesn't help speed)
tried and found that softmax function is not available in current version (remove from documentation?)

Looking forward to comments, ideas and suggestions.

Sanjog

If the restricted parameters in the transformed parameters block are a function of parameters in the parameters block (in fashion that obeys previously declared restrictions) and I place a distribution on the transformed parameters in the model block, then the sampling focus shifts to the transformed parameters.   I know one can't declare local parameters as restricted in the models block, but when may do so in the parameters block, right?  i ask these questions b/c if I understand the outlines of how the stan dev team thinks then i may write smarter .stan scripts.

On Sat, Sep 22, 2012 at 6:59 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
> On Saturday, September 22, 2012 9:24:04 PM UTC-4, tds151 wrote:
> > Why does one have to perform the jacobian increment, manually, when placing  LL' ~ inv_wishart() prior on for L, lower triangular?  Does Stan recognize L as a cholesky factor and therefore not perform the jacobian adjustment to the unrestricted sampling form?  this seem illogical.   how would one have any intuition that they would need to handle the jacobian, themselves?  in particular, for cov_matrix[D] fred;  with fred = LL'; I would not have to perform the adjustment for fred ~ inv_wishart();
>
> This is certainly something that is unique to Stan. I believe the rule is:
>
> 1) If the LHS of a ~ is declared in the parameters block, then the user does NOT need to adjust lp__ with a log absolute Jacobian determinant because Stan will do it automatically if necessary. Similarly, if updating lp__ manually instead of using the ~ syntax, if the variable(s) that are contributing that that lp__ update are declared in the parameters block, then the user does NOT need to further adjust lp__ with a log absolute Jacobian determinant because Stan will do it automatically if necessary
>
> 2) If the LHS of a ~ is declared in the transformed parameters block or is declared as a local variable in the model block, then the user DOES need to adjust lp__ with a log absolute Jacobian determinant. Similarly, if updating lp__ manually instead of using the ~ syntax, if the variable(s) that are contributing that that lp__ update are declared in the transformed parameters block or the model block, then the user DOES need to further adjust lp__ with a log absolute Jacobian determinant.
>
> When the user does this in the .stan file:
>
> parameters{
>   cov_matrix[K] Sigma;
> }
>
> The C++ code utilizes a Cholesky factor (L) --- even though L is not mentioned in the .stan file --- and comes out looking like:
>
> Sigma = L * L.transpose();
> lp__ += a log absolute Jacobian determinant
>
> In other words, the user is utilizing the Cholesky factor without necessarily knowing it.
>
> However, the C++ code is always utilizing unbounded primitive parameters that correspond to the parameters declared in the .stan file. The only exception is
>
> parameters {
>   real mu;
> }
>
> Since mu is unrestricted, there is no need to complicate things with a primitive parameter. In contrast,
>
> parameter {
>   real<lower=0> sigma;
> }
>
> is positive so the C++ will have something like
>
> sigma = exp(sigma_primitive);
> lp__ += a log absolute partial derivative
>
> In other words, a Cholesky factor is the primitive parameter underlying a covariance matrix, just like sigma_primitive is the primitive parameter underlying sigma.
>
> See the chapter of the manual on "Transformations of Variables" for more details.
>
> Ben
>

--
Thank you, Terrance Savitsky

messages.body_plain:
Switching to using bernoulli_logit() is definitely a good idea and may
resolve this issue.  Also, you are declaring a lot of arrays which
aren't needed and vectorization would make your model run much faster.
 E.G.,

for (n in 1:Nmis2){
  real p3lat2[Nmis2];
  p3lat2[n] <- alpha34 + beta34*x34mis2[n];
  Y3[n] ~ bernoulli(Phi(p3lat2[n]));
}

Can just be

for (n in 1:Nmis2){
  Y3[n] ~ bernoulli_logit(alpha34 + beta34*x34mis2[n]);
}

or, with vectorization,

Y3 ~ bernoulli_logit(alpha34 + beta34*x34mis2);

Cheers,
Marcus

I now understand the distinction *when* the user needs to include the (log absolute determinant) jacobian adjustment.  that said, i don't understand why restricted parameters declared in the transformed parameters block if one specifies a distribution in the model block requires the adjustment.  If the restricted parameters in the transformed parameters block are a function of parameters in the parameters block (in fashion that obeys previously declared restrictions) and I place a distribution on the transformed parameters in the model block, then the sampling focus shifts to the transformed parameters.   I know one can't declare local parameters as restricted in the models block, but when may do so in the parameters block, right?  i ask these questions b/c if I understand the outlines of how the stan dev team thinks then i may write smarter .stan scripts.
> >
> > It isn't really true that if you "place a distribution on the transformed parameters in the model block, then the sampling focus shifts to the transformed parameters". In your mind, you might be focusing on the transformed parameters, but from Stan's perspective the sampling is always done on the unbounded, unrestricted, primitive parameters (which the user never even sees). If Stan sampled directly from the transformed parameter space, the sampler (often) might get stuck in a region where the posterior evaluates to zero or is not defined. So, Stan samples from a parameter space where the posterior is defined everywhere and is non-zero everywhere. [In the future, Stan might have an option to bounce around in a transformed parameter subspace, but I doubt that will happen real soon]
> >
> > Maybe you are thinking of a different example, but let me try to clarify using the AR1 example again. If your .stan file were
> >
> > data {
> >   int<lower=1> K;
> > }
> > parameters{
> >   real<lower=0,upper=1> phi;
> >   real<lower=0> sigma_squared;
> > }
> > transformed parameters {
> >   cov_matrix[K] Sigma;
> >   // loops to fill in Sigma as a function of phi and sigma_squared
> > }
> > model {
> >   // informative prior on phi
> >   phi ~ beta(1,2);
> >
> >   // informative prior on sigma_squared
> >   sigma_squared ~ exp(1);
> >
> >   // should NOT have a prior on Sigma
> >   // should NOT have a Jacobian adjustment
> >
> >   // some likelihood of the data as a function of Sigma
> > }
> >
> > Alternatively --- although this makes little substantive sense to me --- you could do
> >
> > data {
> >   int<lower=1> K;
> >   int<lower=K+1> df;
> >   matrix[K,K] scale;
> > }
> > parameters {
> >   real<lower=0,upper=1> phi;
> >   real<lower=0> sigma_squared;
> > }
> > transformed parameters {
> >   cov_matrix[K] Sigma;
> >   // loops to fill in Sigma as a function of phi and sigma_squared
> > }
> > model {
> >   // prior on Sigma with Jacobian adjustment
> >   Sigma ~ wishart(df,scale);
> >   lp__ <- lp__ + SomeJacobianAdjustment;
> >
> >   // should NOT have a prior on phi or sigma_squared
> >
> >   // some likelihood of the data as a function of Sigma
> > }
> >
> > In other words, a Wishart prior on the transformed parameter Sigma implies some prior on phi and sigma_squared (technically, it implies some prior on the primitive parameters underlying phi and sigma_squared but Stan automatically adjusts for the change-of-variables to phi and sigma_squared). The reason why I don't like this on substantive grounds is that it is almost completely opaque as to what a Wishart prior on the transformed parameter Sigma implies about phi and sigma_squared. But it is legal in Stan.
> >
> > Conversely, I do like the first version which has informative priors on phi and sigma_squared (and no prior on Sigma or Jacobian adjustment) because I can easily understand what these two priors entail, even if I might disagree with them. In general, I would say that it is better for a model to put its priors on the parameters that compose a structured covariance matrix than to put a prior on the composed covariance matrix.
> >
> > I would actually go further and say that --- if no other structure is attractive --- compose a covariance matrix as the product of a diagonal matrix of standard deviations, a correlation matrix, and a diagonal matrix of standard deviations. There are lots of choices of priors for standard deviations and Stan has a nice prior distribution for a correlation matrix called lkj_corr that takes a positive shape parameter, eta. If eta = 1, the prior is jointly uniform over all correlation matrices of order K, and to the extent that eta > 1, the prior has a sharper mode at the identity matrix of order K.
> >
> > You see a lot of Wishart and inverse Wishart priors in the literature, but that is often because such priors are necessary for a Gibbs sampler. In Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, conjugacy is not relevant, so Stan users might as well use prior distributions that they believe or at least understand. With Wishart and inverse Wishart priors, the expectation is known but that's about it.
> >
> > Ben

As a start, I would like to implement "spike and slab" prior for logistic regression (which I can extend for the rest of my model if it works):

the spike and slab is as follows:

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] problem with implementing Spike and Slab prior for logistic regression
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] problem with implementing Spike and Slab prior for logistic regression
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kayhan,

At present there is no way to implement spike-and-slab priors in Stan,
because they involve discrete latent variables which cannot be sampled
using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo/NUTS. A later release will include
support for Gibbs sampling for latent discrete variables, but it's not
available right now.

If you don't have many predictors, you might consider summing over all
of the possible settings of gamma, but it'll be quite expensive even
for m in the single digits. Unfortunately, this is one of the few
kinds of models that there aren't really good tricks for sampling in
Stan.

Note also that these models can be painfully slow to mix even with a
well tuned custom sampler. In general, sampling from spike-and-slab
posteriors is tantamount to solving an intractable combinatorial
optimization problem. (Which is why the L1 convex relaxation of the
spike penalty is so popular in the point estimation literature.)

Matt

messages.body_plain:
Hi Kayhan,

No, people often have reasonable success with Gibbs samplers. Usually
the results are no worse than those obtained using variational
inference (although, as usual when comparing MCMC and variational
approaches, Gibbs may take longer). However, it seems as though these
samplers work poorly when it's not possible to integrate out either
the continuous or the discrete parameters, since there are such strong
posterior dependencies between them. For a (non-conjugate) logistic
regression, integrating out the regression coefficients isn't an
option, but you might be able to adapt the approach of Wang&Blei
(2009; http://www.cs.princeton.edu/~blei/papers/WangBlei2009b.pdf and
http://www.cs.princeton.edu/~blei/papers/WangBlei2009c.pdf) if you're
really committed to this model.

Matt

> > > }
> > > model {
> > >   // prior on Sigma with Jacobian adjustment
> > >   Sigma ~ wishart(df,scale);
> > >   lp__ <- lp__ + SomeJacobianAdjustment;
> > >
> > >   // should NOT have a prior on phi or sigma_squared
> > >
> > >   // some likelihood of the data as a function of Sigma
> > > }
> > >
> > > In other words, a Wishart prior on the transformed parameter Sigma implies some prior on phi and sigma_squared (technically, it implies some prior on the primitive parameters underlying phi and sigma_squared but Stan automatically adjusts for the change-of-variables to phi and sigma_squared). The reason why I don't like this on substantive grounds is that it is almost completely opaque as to what a Wishart prior on the transformed parameter Sigma implies about phi and sigma_squared. But it is legal in Stan.
> > >
> > > Conversely, I do like the first version which has informative priors on phi and sigma_squared (and no prior on Sigma or Jacobian adjustment) because I can easily understand what these two priors entail, even if I might disagree with them. In general, I would say that it is better for a model to put its priors on the parameters that compose a structured covariance matrix than to put a prior on the composed covariance matrix.
> > >
> > > I would actually go further and say that --- if no other structure is attractive --- compose a covariance matrix as the product of a diagonal matrix of standard deviations, a correlation matrix, and a diagonal matrix of standard deviations. There are lots of choices of priors for standard deviations and Stan has a nice prior distribution for a correlation matrix called lkj_corr that takes a positive shape parameter, eta. If eta = 1, the prior is jointly uniform over all correlation matrices of order K, and to the extent that eta > 1, the prior has a sharper mode at the identity matrix of order K.
> > >
> > > You see a lot of Wishart and inverse Wishart priors in the literature, but that is often because such priors are necessary for a Gibbs sampler. In Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, conjugacy is not relevant, so Stan users might as well use prior distributions that they believe or at least understand. With Wishart and inverse Wishart priors, the expectation is known but that's about it.
> > >
> > > Ben
> > >
>

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] problem with implementing Spike and Slab prior for logistic regression
messages.body_plain:
Right! If you're willing to compromise on "absolute" sparsity and will
be satisfied with a model that only pushes the betas _close_ to zero,
then you can use all sorts of simple models. One of the simplest is

y           {0,1 }    <--- observed variable

gamma[m]  ~ gamma(0.2, 0.2)      // selector variable

w[m]    ~  Normal(mu[m],sigma[m])   // coefficient
beta[m]   =  gamma[m]*w[m]
y[n] ~ bernoulli(inv_logit(x[n] * beta));

The gamma(0.2, 0.2) prior puts about half of its mass below 0.1, so a
priori this model is saying that you expect many of the betas to be
quite small. (Although none of them will be precisely 0.)

Matt

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for clearing that up; although now I'm feeling pretty stupid for calculating the wrong derivative.   Chapter 26 covers the details of the transformations, but the manual doesn't explicitly mention that parameters defined in the  transformed parameters block on the LHS of ~ need this adjustment to lp__.  However, after writing this, I saw that the example basic_distributions/wishart2x2.stan is an example where the log Jacobian transform is added to lp__.

You're correct, "often" was not the correct adjective. More like "unusual", in which case you wouldn't want syntatic sugar which would make it easier to not think about what you're doing.

Jeff

On Sunday, September 23, 2012 8:58:30 PM UTC-4, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Sunday, September 23, 2012 8:01:01 PM UTC-4, Jeffrey Arnold wrote:
> > Ben,
> >
> > Could you add your discussion of the rules of when the user needs to manually adjust lp__ to the manual? Unless I am missing something, the only discussion is in Ch 16.2 and it only talks about the case in which the LHS of ~ is an expression or lp__ is adjusted directly.
> >
> > And to make sure that I am understanding this correctly, for the following model
> >
> > > parameters {
> > >   real<lower=0> sigma;
> > >   ...
> > > }
> > > transformed parameters {
> > >   real<lower=0> tau;
> > >   tau <- sqrt(sigma);
> > > }
> > > model {
> > >   ...
> > >   tau ~ gamma(0.1, 0.1);
> > >   ...
> > > }
> > requires an extra statement in the model block to adjust the log-posterior
> > > lp__ <-  lp__ + log(0.5 * pow(sigma, -0.5));
>
> You are correct that this model requires the manual adjustment for the change-of-variables. But I think you have it reversed: What is needed is the (log absolute) derivative of the transformation from tau to sigma. Since sigma = tau^2, d sigma / d tau = 2.0 * tau and
>
> lp__ <- lp__ + log(2.0 * tau); // no abs() necessary because already positive
>
> Chapter 26 of 1.0.1 reference manual covers this in the most detail. If this were a real model that utilized both sigma and tau for some reason, I would declare tau as the parameter and sigma as the transformed parameter (or as a local parameter within the model block) if you wanted to place an informative prior on gamma.
>
> > Also this may be a terrible idea, but I'll throw it out there anyways. Since accumulation seems to be used often in Stan, any chance
> > of adding the equivalent of =+ and =-?  I guess that would be <-+ and <-- (the later being definitely suboptimal syntax).
>
> Maybe. I think we are trying to avoid adding syntax unless there is an appreciable benefit. In some languages like C++,
>
> x += 42;
>
> is actually faster than
>
> x = x + 42;
>
> because temporaries are avoided, but that is not really a relevant consideration for the Stan parsing language.
>
> I also wouldn't necessarily agree that accumulation needs to be used "often". It is just that we have been getting a lot of questions from people with big multivariate models, and Stan's implementations of the relevant densities work for everything but are optimal for nothing. So, for now, the fastest way to use multivariate normal / t or inverse / plain Wishart distributions is with hand-optimized accumulation, but it won't be that way forever.
>
> Ben
>

- Bob

On 9/23/12 8:58 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Sunday, September 23, 2012 8:01:01 PM UTC-4, Jeffrey Arnold wrote:
>
>     Ben,
>
>     Could you add your discussion of the rules of when the user needs to manually adjust lp__ to the manual? Unless I am
>     missing something, the only discussion is in Ch 16.2 and it only talks about the case in which the LHS of ~ is an
>     expression or lp__ is adjusted directly.

We'll add a change of variables chapter to the
user's guide.

I want to try to make clear when you can transform
without a Jacobian and when's one necessary.

Which specific issue were you concerned about adding?
Just Ben's two-point post?

>     And to make sure that I am understanding this correctly, for the following model
>
>         parameters {
>            real<lower=0> sigma;
>            ...
>         }
>         transformed parameters {
>            real<lower=0> tau;
>            tau <- sqrt(sigma);
>         }
>         model {
>            ...
>            tau ~ gamma(0.1, 0.1);
>            ...
>         }
>
>     requires an extra statement in the model block to adjust the log-posterior
>
>         lp__ <-  lp__ + log(0.5 * pow(sigma, -0.5));

I'd suggest putting it in the transformed parameters block.

And that is the derivative you need.  I got SO confused
with the directionality of these in our first implementation
of Stan, that I can feel everyone's pain dealing with this
very acutely.  The transform here (at least in the notation
of Gelman et al.'s BDA and our manual) is from tau to
sigma.  The inverse transfrom is from sigma to tau,
and it's the log Jacobian of the inverse that needs to be added.

We'll add some simple univariate, so you should be able to do
this:

     transformed Parameters {
         real<lower=0> tau;
         tau <- sqrt_transform(sigma);
     }

or go even further and eliminate the intermediate variable and
just use this:

     model {
        ...
        sqrt_transform(sigma) ~ gamma(0.1,0.1);

The sqrt_transform() function bring in the Jacobian
itself behind the scenes.  The discussion we've been having is
how to compose these in multivariate settings because we can't easily compute
and then auto-dif Jacobians (we can do one or the other, but
not second-order derivatives).

>     Also this may be a terrible idea, but I'll throw it out there anyways. Since accumulation seems to be used often in
>     Stan, any chance
>     of adding the equivalent of =+ and =-?  I guess that would be <-+ and <-- (the later being definitely suboptimal
>     syntax).

Yes, that's on the to-do list.  The usual syntax
in C, Java, etc. for compound assignment has the operator
first.  The statement

    a += b;

has the same effect on a as:

    a = a + b;

Syntactically and semantically it's no issue to add,
but I'm uncertain what to call it given how ugly
"+<-" looks.  But that's what it'll have to be.

An alternative would be:

   lp_increment(x);

to stand in for:

   lp <- lp + x;

Thoughts?

> Maybe. I think we are trying to avoid adding syntax unless there is an appreciable benefit.

I think there's a benefit to this just as in C++.
It's cleaner and clearer.  I just haven't added it
because our to-do list is already a mile long.

 > In some languages like C++,
>
> x += 42;
>
> is actually faster than
>
> x = x + 42;
>
> because temporaries are avoided, but that is not really a relevant consideration for the Stan parsing language.

It's relevant insofar as we translate

   lp__ <- lp__ + x;

into C++ as:

   lp__ = lp__ + x;

I'm guessing the compilers are good enough to figure
out this can be optimized as well as:

   lp += x;

> I also wouldn't necessarily agree that accumulation needs to be used "often". It is just that we have been getting a lot
> of questions from people with big multivariate models, and Stan's implementations of the relevant densities work for
> everything but are optimal for nothing. So, for now, the fastest way to use multivariate normal / t or inverse / plain
> Wishart distributions is with hand-optimized accumulation, but it won't be that way forever.

I want to have this available for sums in loops, too.

- Bob

messages.subject: RStan suport for RStudio?
messages.body_plain:
RStan's not working for at least one Mac user
under RStudio.  Has anyone gotten RStan working
in any version of RStudio?  On Mac OS X?

The issue at hand is whether RStan should support
RStudio.  It's not part of either Stan or RStan,
so the answer can conceivably be "no".

   Option 1:  leave it up to users.

   Option 2:  figure out the current user problem,
      test future releases against RStudio, and provide
      install instructions if they're non-trivial.

I have no idea how widepspread RStudio use is,
but it should be part of our decision, along with
how easy/hard it would be for users to switch back
and forth between RStudio and R in the terminal or
R GUI.

I don't personally use IDEs for (at least) three reasons:
(a) they're just one more thing to misconfigure in
the tool chain, and (b) they're hard to script,
and (c) I'd rather type than point and click.

For now, I'm going to put the issue with RStan into
our issue tracker, but I'll leave it to others to
solve.  We can discuss whether we want to support
RStudio at the Stan meeting tomorrow.

- Bob

> posterior need to be made.  When I first read Ben's post, I went back through all my models to make sure I hadn't used a
> sampling statement with any transformed variables. Thankfully, I hadn't. But when writing them I didn't know that it
> would have been a problem,even though I was aware that if I made manual adjustments to the log posterior or transformed
> a variable in the model block I would likely have to add the log Jacobian.

OK -- will do.

I need to make sure a warning gets printed if anyone
tries to use a transformed parameter on the left
side of a sampling statement.  I think that would go
a long way to helping people out.

>      >     requires an extra statement in the model block to adjust the log-posterior
>      >
>      >         lp__ <-  lp__ + log(0.5 * pow(sigma, -0.5));
>
>     I'd suggest putting it in the transformed parameters block.
>
>
> Why in the transformed parameters block? Is this for style or efficiency?

Just style.  The Jacobian adjustment only depends on
the transformed parameter declarations.  In general,
it's better to use things near where they're declared
for program clarity.

Now, where we fall down on that big time is by requiring
variable declarations in a block at the top!

>     An alternative would be:
>
>         lp_increment(x);
>
>     to stand in for:
>
>         lp <- lp + x;
>

>

I'm not sure what you mean by flexibility, but
given that

   lp_increment(x)
   ===  lp__ +<- x
   ===  lp__ <- lp__ + x;

the operator pileup +<- is definitely more general,
but the basic assignment <- is most general.

 > I think somewhere on the TODO list is a way to automatically calculate
> likelihoods / deviance.

For that, we'd need to break the model apart into
a prior and likelihood component.  That would actually
be pretty easy syntactically and in terms of the
translation, but then it'd be up to the user to get
the right things in the right places.

>  From the user's perspective, a reasonable implementation would be to add a logical flag on sampling statements and
> lp_increment()
> in order to increment a likelihood variable in addition to lp__.  But I understand that this feature is nowhere near the
> top of the queue, and is probably
> a bad idea for reasons that i can't think of right now.

I like having two blocks, but one way we originally
thought about doing declarations was with flags.

- Bob

messages.subject: calling STAN as a black box
messages.subject_clean: calling STAN as a black box
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm interested in using STAN as a component of a much more complicated sampler.  My intended model has a nonparametric Bayesian hierarchy. It has lots of discrete assignments, and so representing things entirely as continuous parameters isn't possible. However, there are some non-conjugate updates to continuous parameters that I think STAN would be great for, since it has (1) fast C code, and (2) good mixing via NUTS.

Is it possible to use STAN in this way? To be concrete, suppose I have fixed data, discrete variables "Z" that I need to sample using my own custom methods, and continuous variables "theta" that I want STAN to sample. Ideally, the pseudocode (in high-level syntax) would look something like

for iter = 1:Niter
> Z = SampleMyCustomDiscreteParams( data, theta )
> theta = SampleContinuousParamsViaSTAN(  data,  Z, theta)
end

Right now, it looks like I could define a STAN model for theta given fixed Z,data.  This could be compiled, and called from my larger sampler as a "black box".  However,  this "black box" would write output to a csv file, and I'd have to do expensive file IO to get the samples back into my program.  Is there a way to bypass the "write to CSV" part of stan and have it return values directly?  I recognize this probably isn't easy, but hoping it might be possible.

Alternatively, I suppose I could try to directly implement the NUTS algorithm for the task at hand, but it seems a shame to reinvent the wheel when the code for STAN has been optimized and crafted so carefully.

Thanks for any help!
Mike

We've been thinking about similar issues for blocking
HMC parameters, adding Gibbs, etc.  So far, there's not
an easy mechanism for doing this.

> Is it possible to use STAN in this way? To be concrete, suppose I have fixed data, discrete variables "Z" that I need to
> sample using my own custom methods, and continuous variables "theta" that I want STAN to sample. Ideally, the pseudocode
> (in high-level syntax) would look something like
> for iter = 1:Niter
>
>     Z = SampleMyCustomDiscreteParams( data, theta )
>
>     theta = SampleContinuousParamsViaSTAN(  data,  Z, theta)
>
> end
>
> Right now, it looks like I could define a STAN model for theta given fixed Z,data.  This could be compiled, and called
> from my larger sampler as a "black box".

Hopefully we can be a bit more transparent than that.

 > However,  this "black box" would write output to a csv file, and I'd have to
> do expensive file IO to get the samples back into my program.  Is there a way to bypass the "write to CSV" part of stan
> and have it return values directly?  I recognize this probably isn't easy, but hoping it might be possible.

Check out the C++ generated when a Stan model is compiled
via stanc.  This has some methods in it that you can use,
including one to write the parameters into a std::vector<double>
without going through file I/O (that's how the R interface works
without invoking file I/O).

Then you should treat the custom sampler as producing data
for the Stan model.  You'd have to write something yourself
to read the data in.

One issue is how adaptation would work in this setting.
NUTS is set up to use the warmup samples to tune the
step sizes.  This might still work with changing "data".
We haven't tried it yet with a combined discrete sampler.

> Alternatively, I suppose I could try to directly implement the NUTS algorithm for the task at hand, but it seems a shame
> to reinvent the wheel when the code for STAN has been optimized and crafted so carefully.

There's also the auto-dif.  NUTS is easy in terms of
implementation compared to the variable transforms plus
auto-dif.

- Bob

I will write some in the instruction for RStudio users.

What is more, please check if R_ARCH is set if you want to install rstan in RStudio.  If it is not, for some reason, function install.packages will take my 64bits RStudio as 32bits and then compile 32bits RStan.  I guess then it is problematic to load rstan.

So if using RStudio, the first thing to do after start RStudio is to check R_ARCH is set appropriately.  I strongly recommend at least installing rstan in official R app's.

--
Jiqiang

messages.body_snippet: I have a zero-inflated Poisson model problem that I implemented in JAGS.  The data is about species response to environmental change.  This is a mixed model with density p(y) = pi+(1-pi)exp(-lambda),

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Zero inflated Poisson model
messages.body_plain:
On 9/26/12 11:44 AM, Song wrote:
 > I have a zero-inflated Poisson model problem that I implemented in JAGS.

 > ...

 > I tried to use
 > Stan this week and it worked for the single species model, but with very different results.

Thanks for trying it out.

There are two issues.  A bug on our end and an
error in coding your model.  We're fixing the bug
for 1.0.2, but luckily in this case, recoding the model
with constraints will fix the problem in 1.0.1.

The model coding problem is that need to declare the parameters to
have constraints that match their truncations:

 > ...

 >                    parameters{
 >                      real alpha[2];
 >                      real beta[3];
 >                    }
 >                    model{

...

 >                      alpha[1] ~ normal(10,100);
 >                      alpha[2] ~ normal(10,100)T[0,];
 >
 >                      beta[1] ~ normal(0, 100);
 >                      beta[2] ~ normal(0, 100)T[0,];
 >                      beta[3] ~ normal(0, 100)T[-1,];

This means you need to define alpha[2], beta[2], and beta[3]
with constraints.  This isn't directly possible in a Stan
array, which requires the same constraint on every entry.

So in this case, I'd just recode as

parameters
   real alpha1;
   real<lower=0> alpha2;
   real beta1;
   real<lower=0> beta2;
   real<lower=-1> beta3;

 >
 >                      for(i in 1:NOBS) {
 >                        lambda[i] <- exp(beta[1]-beta[2]*x[i]+beta[3]*log(x[i]));
 >                        pi[i] <- inv_logit(alpha[1] + alpha[2]*x[i]);

It's a bit more efficient to define lambda and pi
to be scalars and reuse them (they don't need
to be arrays).

 >                        lp__ <- lp__ + if_else(iszero[i], log(pi[i] + (1-pi[i]) * exp(-lambda[i])),
 >                                               log1m(pi[i])+poisson_log(Y[i], lambda[i]));

If lambda[i] gets too small (< -800 or so), the
exp(-lambda[i]) will overflow.  In general, log_sum_exp
can be used to avoid the overflow:

   log(pi[i] + (1-pi[i]) * exp(-lambda[i]))

   ==>

   log_sum_exp(log(pi[i]),
               log1m(pi[i]) - lambda[i]);

    == log(exp(log(pi[i]))
           + exp(log(1 - pi[i])*exp(-lambda[i])))

Otherwise, everything looks OK on first glance.

> ...

> When using Stan, I wrote R script shown below. The estimated betas are close, but truncation is ignored.

Exactly!  This is a bug in the current version of truncation
(which I'm about to fix).  It doesn't check if the
values are outside the truncation range and reject.

I didn't think about that implementing it the first
time because the right way to implement it is with
the constraints.  So if you put the constraints in,
it should pay attention to the constraints and do
the right thing.

 > ...

> The estimated
> alphas are very different.  I must have done something wrong

Your model should've worked as is, albeit slowly
and with the danger of getting stuck outside the
truncated support.

Version 1.0.2 should do the right thing with your
existing model, but it'll be relatively slow to sample.

The right way to code it for 1.0.1 and 1.0.2 is with
constraints.

> and would appreciate some help.  Thank you very much.

Thanks again for letting us know and sending a detailed
error report.    Please let us know if adding constraints
fixes the problem.  It should.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Zero inflated Poisson model
messages.body_plain:
This isn't a 1.0.1 vs. 1.0.2 issue if you have the
transforms matching your truncations.  (I should've
also pointed out that if the truncation points are
constant, you don't even need the truncations -- the
probabilty is still right up to a proportion without it.)

Are you letting Stan do the initializations or
doing them yourself?  If you are, the inits need to
be in the support or you'll get the error you report
because no step size will get the particle moving.

You can try running with the test_grad option to
see if the initialization is OK -- it'll print out
the unconstrained (transformed) initial values along with
the gradients  computed by auto-dif and by finite diffs.
(The unconstrained params come in the same order as
the parameter declarations.)

The partials in the gradient should all be finite, or
there's a problem with the model specification at the
initialization point.

If you run this and still have problems that aren't
due to inits, could you send us a copy of the current model
and data, either to the list or to st...@mc-stan.org?

- Bob

Bob,

Thanks for looking into this for me. The data file is attached. I always generate initial values to make sure that the model start from a point acceptable.  I tried init="random" and got the same error message.

Song

Data <- dget("bosdata.Rdata")

bugs.in <http://bugs.in> <- function(y=Data$y15, x=Data$NUII, n.chains=3){
  n <- length(y)
  iszero <- as.numeric(y==0)
  bugs.ini <- list()
  bugs.data <- list(NOBS=n, Y=y, x=x, iszero=iszero)
  for (i in 1:n.chains)

    bugs.ini [[i]] <- list(alpha1=runif(1),alpha2=runif(1),
                           beta1=runif(1),beta2=runif(1),beta3=runif(1))
  bugs.para <- c("alpha1","alpha2","beta1","beta2","beta3")

  return(list(data=bugs.data, inits=bugs.ini, para=bugs.para,
              n.chains=n.chains,
              model="
                  data{
                    int<lower=0> NOBS;
                    real<lower=0> x[NOBS];
                    int<lower=0> Y[NOBS];
                    int iszero[NOBS];
                  }

                  parameters{
                    real alpha1;
                    real<lower=0> alpha2;
                    real beta1;
                    real<lower=0> beta2;
                    real<lower=-1> beta3;
                  }

                  model{
                    real lambda;
                    real pi;

                    alpha1 ~ normal(10,100);
                    alpha2 ~ normal(10,100);

                    beta1 ~ normal(0, 100);
                    beta2 ~ normal(0, 100);
                    beta3 ~ normal(0, 100);

                    for(i in 1:NOBS) {
                      lambda <- exp(beta1-beta2*x[i]+beta3*log(x[i]));
                      pi <- inv_logit(alpha1 + alpha2*x[i]);
                      lp__ <- lp__ + if_else(iszero[i], log_sum_exp(log(pi) , log1m(pi)-lambda),
                                             log1m(pi)+poisson_log(Y[i], lambda));
                    }
                  }
                  generated quantities{
                    real lambda;
                    real pi;
                    real logitEC50;

                    logitEC50 <- -alpha1/alpha2;
                    for(i in 1:NOBS){
                      lambda <- exp(beta1-beta2*x[i]+beta3*log(x[i]));
                      pi <- inv_logit(alpha1 + alpha2*x[i]);

                    }
                 }
                "))
  }

input.to.bugs <- bugs.in <http://bugs.in>()
n.chains <- input.to.bugs$n.chains

n.iter <- 100000

n.keep <- 2000
thin <- max(c(1,floor((n.iter)*n.chains/n.keep)))

fit <- stan(model_code=input.to.bugs$model,
            data=input.to.bugs$data,init=input.to.bugs$inits,

            pars=input.to.bugs$para,test_grad=T,
            iter=n.iter, thin=thin, chains=n.chains)

messages.subject: Slow rstan extract method
messages.body_plain:
The extract method in rstan has been frustrating me, as it appears to get rapidly slower as the @sim results get bigger in the stanfit object. I noticed this, because I fit a series of models in Stan and then went about simulating predictions from each. The computations bogged down in the larger models, and some investigation revealed the delay was happening inside rstan::extract.

I ended up writing my own faster extract function (see below), so worked around the problem. But if it's easy to fix it, might be worth adding to the to-do list.

Here's my special-purpose extract that performs well (but is not as flexible as extract), along with some system.time results, to see how big the delay can be.

fastx <- function( object , par ) {
    begin <- attr(object@sim[[1]][[1]],"args")$warmup + 1
    end <- attr(object@sim[[1]][[1]],"args")$iter
    object@sim[[1]][[1]][[ par ]][begin:end]
}

Timed below for extracting 5000 non-warmup samples from a single chain, for a single parameter. The model has a few thousands parameters, so a big @sim object.

> system.time( mean( fastx( fit , "mu[1]" ) ) )

   user  system elapsed

  0.004   0.001   0.004

>

> system.time( mean( extract( fit , "mu[1]" , inc_warmup=FALSE ) ) )

   user  system elapsed

  0.411   0.293   1.229

messages.body_plain:
If you want help with models, please send
the following files as attachments with a
description of the problem you're having.

1.  model file

2.  data file

3.  (optional) inits file

The data file can be created from R using
dump(list("var1",...)) or even better yet, using
stan_rdump() from the rstan package.

Make sure the data file has ALL the variables
listed in the data block of the model.

The reason I suggest this format of model and data
rather than an R program is that most of the developers,
including me, don't use Stan through RStan, and it's
also easier to instrument the code directly rather than
having to repackage and reinstall for R.  Also, the
above format is easy to use through RStan, so it
works for everyone.

Thanks,

- Bob

>     successively augment lp__ .   I wanted to confirm that "declare once, use many" is okay for local variables in the
>     Models section.   I encountered an example in response to a post that repeatedly re-declared the local variable
>     before each re-use occasion, prompting this question.

It's not really a redeclaration per se.

It's usually good style to put declarations near
where they're used because it makes the program
easier to understand (less scanning).  An exception to
this rule is for compound structures such as arrays
or matrices, but only when they are filled elementwise.
For this case, preallocating outside of a block where
they're repeatedly used can be more efficient.

I added a style guide appendix and I'll put a
note in there about this case with some examples.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] poor mixing of variance components
messages.body_plain:
Hi Toby,

I'd recommend trying to run the sampler for longer as a first
step—it's possible that the warmup phase wasn't long enough to
accurately estimate the scale of the parameters.

Also, part of the problem may be that the correct answer is fairly
deep in the left tail of the inverse-gamma prior, which is very light.
So the posterior over the between group variance will have a very
light left tail. And NUTS and HMC can sometimes have trouble with
light-tailed distributions (Roberts and Tweedie, 1996). You might have
better luck if you used a less informative prior.

Best,
Matt

> was centered to mean zero but y1 was not for some reason. I found that with such data Stan does not start sampling and

> data/inits dump file and model file are attached. I would appreciate any help on this.
>

> Keiichi

> P.S.
> I've tried to fit several models (a state-space model with multi_normal distributions/ a standard random wark model with
> a multi_normal distribution/ a standard multi_normal model/ a state_space model with normal distributions) to same data
> but this problem occurs only when I fitted state-space models. Attached files are the code for the state-space model
> with multi_normal distributions and associating data/inits, but if someone needs other models and their data/inits I can
> share them as well.

Thanks for the clear error report -- it really helps
to have everything at hand.

I don't know anything about state-space models, but it
looks like a pretty straightforward time-series arrangement.

Your problem is probably related to the uniform
samples for t=1.  Because y_dash[1,n] is a parameter, there's nothing
keeping it bounded between min_y[n] and max_y[n].  The uniform
doesn't do that -- it only evaluates the probability.
If it gets out of bounds, you'll run into the problem
you see because no step size is small enough to move
out of a point not in the support of the probability function.

For now, I'd suggest option 1:

1.  get rid of the uniform sampling for t=1.  If the
y_dash[1,n] stay in range, it doesn't do anything because
we only compute probabilities up to a proportion and
so there's no contribution from a uniform with constant
bounds.

You could also try option 2:

2.  declare in the parameters block that y_dash[1,n] is
bounded between min_y[n] and max_y[n].  Unfortunately, we
haven't yet added bounds constraints to vectors and matrices,
and even wehn we do, it's not going to support declaring each
entry in a data structure to have different bounds.  So for
now, you'd have to:

    b.  declare a 2D array with those bounds

directly, but even then, it won't support varying bounds on
different components of the structure.

option Jiqiang added to RStan in 1.0.2.  It'll dump all
the unconstrained params and their gradients at the init
point.  If the initial state's
illegal, you'll see NaN or infinite values.

I'm out of town now, but can look at this in more detail
next week when I get back if nobody else gets there first.

- Bob

messages.subject: Help with multivariate ordered logistic model
messages.subject_clean: Help with multivariate ordered logistic model
messages.body_plain:
I have 2 sets of multivariate ordinal responses, y1[i,d] and y2[i,d], modeled as ordered_logistic with intrinsic traits, c1[i,d] and c2[i,d] for d = 1, ..., D.   The intrinsic traits are connected by sharing hierarchical multivariate random effects.  For example, there is D x M, Delta[T],  and Phi[S] where d = 1, ... D are multivariate dimension and m = 1, ..., (M=2) are alternate measurement modes.   Then c1[i,d] = Delta[teacher1[i]][d,1] + Phi[section1[i]][d,1] and  c2[i,d] = Delta[teacher2[i]][d,2] + Phi[section2[i]][d,2].  Each latent response has ordered cutpoints, D x ncut, lim1 and lim2.

The model crashes during sampling, with the following error message:

SAMPLING FOR MODEL 'modelFAcum_lkj' NOW (CHAIN 1).
Error in sampler$call_sampler(args_list[[i]]) :
  Error in function stan::prob::ordered_logistic(N4stan5agrad3varE): Location parameter is 1.#QNAN:0, but must be finite!

This indicates to me that one or more of the ordered cutpoint values spins off to infinity.   In the attached model, the cutpoints are defined such that the first is fixed to 0 as a hard constraint, which is necessary to establish location identifiability.  (A soft constraint of an informative prior isn't sufficient).   That said, I ran a simpler version, taking away this constraint to see if the problem went away, but it didn't - I received the exact same error message.

The model section includes statement blocks for each of the hierarchical multivariate random effects.  lp__ is incremented using a matrix normal distribution, which is the equivalent of vectorizing the parameters and using a structured kronecker product of D x D and M x M covariance matrices.   The first set of random effect parameters, Delta, composes the D x D covariance under a factor analytic structure, where cov(Delta) = Lambda * Lambda' + Theta, for D x K, Lambda where K < D.   A lower triangular structure is enforced for Lambda (for rotation identification) by reading a binary "pick" matrix, B, filled with 0's and 1's that multiplies against a D x K matrix of parameters, Lambda_s, with each element sampled from a standard normal.

My intuition is that placing informative priors on the cutpoints won't fix the problem, but maybe all parameters need relatively informative priors due to the model complexity to accomplish joint sampling.  I let Stan generate initial parameter values, which should be fine (under the declared constraints).  That said, I'm now experimenting with inputing my own initial values.

This model is a first step to see if i'm able to get Stan to work.   I'm intending to replace the ordered_logistic construction with a latent response.  I've created another script that employs tricks generously offered from Stan developers to get around the lack of functionality for by-element truncation points.   Such a construction will eventually allow me to generalize the logit link function to something semi-parametric (e.g. multimodal).   I have successfully implemented similar models in JAGS, but for M = 1 mode.   That said, I have combined datasets in JAGS under this type of model that share portions of multivariate random effect parameters in a similar fashion.   Because JAGS requires conjugacy for covariance matrices (and doesn't allow direct updates to the joint log probability) I would have to define D*M x D*M unstructured covariance matrices to use JAGS.

Thanks for your time and help.  Terrance

--
Thank you, Terrance Savitsky

Hi Terrance,

For help debugging models --- particularly for models as complicated as this --- it would help if you could narrow the problem down yourself as much as possible before posting. Here is what I did to figure it out. If you haven't already done so, definitely install version 1.0.2 because it introduces the print() function.

I added these print lines to your .stan file:
        /* Formulate c1[i,d] and c2[i,d], mean of latent response or multi-variate trait in ordered_logistic model */
        print("Delta= ", Delta[teacher1[1]][1,1]);
        print("Phi= ", Phi[section1[1]][1,1]);
        print("Theta= ", Theta[session1[1]][1,1]);
        print("Zeta= ", Zeta[session_rater1[1]][1,1]);
        print("Beta_mean= ", Beta_mean[rater1[1]][1,1]);
        for( i in 1:N1 ) for( d in 1:D ) c1[i,d] <- Delta[teacher1[i]][d,1] + Phi[section1[i]][d,1] + Theta[session1[i]][d,1] + Zeta[session_rater1[i]][d,1] + Beta_mean[rater1[i]][d,1];
        for( i in 1:N2 ) for( d in 1:D ) c2[i,d] <- Delta[teacher2[i]][d,2] + Phi[section2[i]][d,2] + Theta[session2[i]][d,2] + Zeta[session_rater2[i]][d,2] + Beta_mean[rater2[i]][d,2];

I then compiled compiled with -g (you may have to add that in the Makefile) and O=0 and ran it under gdb

goodrich@CYBERPOWERPC:/tmp/Terrance$ gdb --args ./modelFAcum_lkj --data=datstan.Rdump
GNU gdb (GDB) 7.4.1-debian

(gdb) catch throw

Starting program: /tmp/Terrance/modelFAcum_lkj --data=datstan.Rdump
[Thread debugging using libthread_db enabled]
Using host libthread_db library "/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libthread_db.so.1".
Delta= 1.04147
Phi= -1.2006
Theta= 1.17
Zeta= 1.49939
Beta_mean= nan
Catchpoint 1 (exception thrown), 0x00007ffff791db90 in __cxa_throw () from /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libstdc++.so.6

At this point, you could fool around in gdb to investigate further; Google shows lots of HOWTOs for gdb.

But the print() statements in the .stan file indicate that the elements of c1 (and c2) are nan because the elements of Beta_mean are nan, which happens because you attempted to use it before filling it:

goodrich@CYBERPOWERPC:/tmp/Terrance$ grep -n Beta_mean modelFAcum_lkj.stan
79:     matrix[D,M] Beta_mean[Rr];
97:     print("Beta_mean= ", Beta_mean[rater1[1]][1,1]);
98:     for( i in 1:N1 ) for( d in 1:D ) c1[i,d] <- Delta[teacher1[i]][d,1] + Phi[section1[i]][d,1] + Theta[session1[i]][d,1] + Zeta[session_rater1[i]][d,1] + Beta_mean[rater1[i]][d,1];
99:     for( i in 1:N2 ) for( d in 1:D ) c2[i,d] <- Delta[teacher2[i]][d,2] + Phi[section2[i]][d,2] + Theta[session2[i]][d,2] + Zeta[session_rater2[i]][d,2] + Beta_mean[rater2[i]][d,2];
118:    for( r in 1:Rr ) Beta_mean[r] <- Beta[r] + mean_Beta;
228:    /* functions of multivariate hierarchical parameters, Delta, Phi, Theta, Zeta, Beta_mean */

So, I think line 118 (maybe 113 in your original .stan file) needs to be moved farther up or something.

Ben

D are multivariate dimension and m = 1, ..., (M=2) are alternate measurement modes.   Then c1[i,d] = Delta[teacher1[i]][d,1] + Phi[section1[i]][d,1] and  c2[i,d] = Delta[teacher2[i]][d,2] + Phi[section2[i]][d,2].  Each latent response has ordered cutpoints, D x ncut, lim1 and lim2.

> > >
> > > The model section includes statement blocks for each of the hierarchical multivariate random effects.  lp__ is incremented using a matrix normal distribution, which is the equivalent of vectorizing the parameters and using a structured kronecker product of D x D and M x M covariance matrices.   The first set of random effect parameters, Delta, composes the D x D covariance under a factor analytic structure, where cov(Delta) = Lambda * Lambda' + Theta, for D x K, Lambda where K < D. I've created another script that employs tricks generously offered from Stan developers to get around the lack of functionality for by-element truncation points. On Sat, Sep 29, 2012 at 2:32 AM, FUKAYA Keiichi <fuka...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi Bob,
>
> thank you very much for the detailed comments -- they were very
> helpful and let me notice how the Stan code can be different from that
> in WinBUGS (in WinBUGS I think priors should be specified for t = 1
> and they would keep parameters bounded).
>
> The option 1 you suggested fixed the problem. Also, letting min_y very
> small and max_y very large worked as well (although this should not be
> a smart solution, it made me confident what you explained was
> correct).
>
> Regards,
> Keiichi
>
>
> 2012/9/29 Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com>:
> > On 9/27/12 10:26 PM, FUKAYA Keiichi wrote:
> >>
> >> Hi all,
> >>
> >> I've been trying to fit a state-space model of the vector time-series in
> >> RStan. I had two variables, y1 and y2, where y2
> >> was centered to mean zero but y1 was not for some reason. I found that
> >> with such data Stan does not start sampling and
> >> shows the following error message:
> >>
> >>      No acceptably small step size could be found. Perhaps the posterior
> >> is not continuous?
> >>
> >> but it works when y1 was centered. I guess there should be something wrong
> >> in my code but I couldn't identify it. The
> >> data/inits dump file and model file are attached. I would appreciate any
> >> help on this.
> >>
> >> Regards,
> >> Keiichi
> >>
> >> P.S.
> >> I've tried to fit several models (a state-space model with multi_normal
> >> distributions/ a standard random wark model with
> >> a multi_normal distribution/ a standard multi_normal model/ a state_space
> >> model with normal distributions) to same data
> >> but this problem occurs only when I fitted state-space models. Attached
> >> files are the code for the state-space model
> >> with multi_normal distributions and associating data/inits, but if someone
> >> needs other models and their data/inits I can
> >> share them as well.
> >
> >
> > Thanks for the clear error report -- it really helps
> > to have everything at hand.
> >
> > I don't know anything about state-space models, but it
> > looks like a pretty straightforward time-series arrangement.
> >
> > Your problem is probably related to the uniform
> > samples for t=1.  Because y_dash[1,n] is a parameter, there's nothing
> > keeping it bounded between min_y[n] and max_y[n].  The uniform
> > doesn't do that -- it only evaluates the probability.
> > If it gets out of bounds, you'll run into the problem
> > you see because no step size is small enough to move
> > out of a point not in the support of the probability function.
> >
> > For now, I'd suggest option 1:
> >
> > 1.  get rid of the uniform sampling for t=1.  If the
> > y_dash[1,n] stay in range, it doesn't do anything because
> > we only compute probabilities up to a proportion and
> > so there's no contribution from a uniform with constant
> > bounds.
> >
> > You could also try option 2:
> >
> > 2.  declare in the parameters block that y_dash[1,n] is
> > bounded between min_y[n] and max_y[n].  Unfortunately, we
> > haven't yet added bounds constraints to vectors and matrices,
> > and even wehn we do, it's not going to support declaring each
> > entry in a data structure to have different bounds.  So for
> > now, you'd have to:
> >
> >    a.  fix an overall bound for the y_dash not dependent on n
> >
> >    b.  declare a 2D array with those bounds
> >
> >    c.  copy the entries into a transformed parameter vector
> >
> > I'm about to add the code that'll let you declare a bound
> > directly, but even then, it won't support varying bounds on
> > different components of the structure.
> >
> > You can diagnose some of these problems using the test_grad
> > option Jiqiang added to RStan in 1.0.2.  It'll dump all
> > the unconstrained params and their gradients at the init
> > point.  If the initial state's
> > illegal, you'll see NaN or infinite values.
> >
> > I'm out of town now, but can look at this in more detail
> > next week when I get back if nobody else gets there first.
> >
> > - Bob

On Sat, Sep 29, 2012 at 10:19 PM, Jeffrey Arnold
<jeffrey...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi Bob,
>
> Does log_uniform() return -Inf if the value is outside the support of the
> distribution?

Hi Jeffrey,

uniform_log() currently throws an exception if the value is outside
the support of the distribution. We are in the process of working
through all the distributions so they return -Inf when outside the
support of the distribution.

In Stan, under most situations, both behaviors results in rejecting
the sample. The way it is currently implemented, it will produce a
non-fatal error message. Once we change the behavior, the error
message will disappear.

Daniel

Sorry. I was foolishly thinking that by adding -Infinity to the log posterior, it would effectively act like truncation, albeit inefficient truncation. But then I went back and read the old thread on truncation; I should have done that first :-)
Jeff

On Sat, Sep 29, 2012 at 10:41 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
> On Sat, Sep 29, 2012 at 10:19 PM, Jeffrey Arnold
> <jeffrey...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi Bob,
> >
> > Does log_uniform() return -Inf if the value is outside the support of the
> > distribution?
>
> Hi Jeffrey,
>
> uniform_log() currently throws an exception if the value is outside
> the support of the distribution. We are in the process of working
> through all the distributions so they return -Inf when outside the
> support of the distribution.
>
> In Stan, under most situations, both behaviors results in rejecting
> the sample. The way it is currently implemented, it will produce a
> non-fatal error message. Once we change the behavior, the error
> message will disappear.
>
>
> Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Does any model work (e.g. the example in ?stan):

     library(rstan)
     scode <- "
     parameters {
       real y[2];
     }
     model {
       y[1] ~ normal(0, 1);
       y[2] ~ double_exponential(0, 2);
     }
     "
     fit1 <- stan(model_code = scode, iter = 10, verbose = FALSE)
     print(fit1)
     fit2 <- stan(fit = fit1, iter = 10000, verbose = FALSE)

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] discrete parameters hack
messages.body_plain:
It could work in theory (i.e., as the chain length goes to infinity it should converge because detailed balance and ergodicity should still hold for the HMC transition kernel), but the sampler is likely to perform very poorly for finite chains.  Rejection rates will be high near the rounding boundaries making it hard to transition between discrete parameter values resulting in poor mixing which may be very hard to diagnose.  It's also likely that the stepsize adaptation of NUTS2 may behave badly near rounding boundaries.

Personally, I wouldn't recommend people use it for real work due to the likelihood of incorrect results that may be hard to notice.

Cheers,
Marcus
